events.text: The pass between the two valleys is a notch in the ridge, a road of packed earth and roots, a stone cairn at the top where travellers add a pebble and spit for luck. The old tiger who held it died some winters ago; its bones are white in the gully below the bend. At the foot of the road, on both sides, there is a roadside inn where woodcutters and salt carriers wait in the yard until they are ten, because nobody crosses this pass in fewer. Nobody has told you it is yours now. Nobody needs to.

choices.text: Take the flat rock above the bend, where the old tiger sat

effects.log: The rock is still warm from somebody else, a long time ago. You lie down on it. Below you the road goes round the bend and out of sight, and every human who crosses must pass under your chin.

choices.text: Walk the road itself, by night, and learn every smell on it

effects.log: Charcoal, salt, horse, rice straw, fear, old blood at the bend, tobacco at the cairn. By spring you can tell from the wind which inn a traveller slept at.

choices.text: Let the ten see you at dusk, once, so the whole valley knows

effects.log: Ten woodcutters stop dead. Nine of them drop their loads. The tenth, who is very old, takes off his hat and bows, and that night both inns know the pass has a tiger again.

events.text: Dusk, and the ten are crossing: A-frames loaded with pine, torches, a gong that the first man beats every few steps to tell the mountain they are coming. The old people say a tiger takes the last in a line, so nobody wants to be last. Tonight the last is a boy of twelve with a limp, who cannot keep up, and the line does not wait for him.

choices.text: Walk behind the boy all the way down, so nothing else on the mountain takes the last

effects.log: The boy hears something big breathing behind him for the whole descent and does not dare look round. At the inn he swears the tiger followed him. He is right. It is the safest walk he will ever take.

choices.text: Sit on your rock and count them, as they count each other

effects.log: One, two, three, the gong, the boy. They count heads at the cairn, and again at the bottom, and so do you. Humans, it turns out, are mostly afraid of the gap between the numbers.

choices.text: Take the last one. That is what the old people say tigers do

effects.log: The torches go round the bend, and the limping boy does not. The line counts nine at the bottom. The next night a child's voice on the pass calls the woodcutters by name, one by one, and a ghost walks behind you.

events.text: Long after dark, one lantern on the road: {npc}, a salt peddler with a back-load of grey sea salt, crossing alone because salt fetches twice the price in the next valley this year and the ten will not leave till morning. {He} beats a little brass gong at every bend and sings, badly, to the mountain, to tell it {he} is only a peddler and very thin.

choices.text: Sit up on the rock where the wolves can see you, and let {him} pass

mem.note: sat on the rock where the wolves could see, and let me cross

effects.log: Somewhere in the dark the wolves see your eyes and change their minds. {npc} sees them too and sings louder, and crosses, and never knows the eyes were the reason {he} lived.

choices.text: Step out onto the road and look at {him}

mem.note: met the tiger of the pass and lived

ok.log: {npc} stops singing. Then, very slowly, {he} unties a twist of salt from the load, sets it on the road, bows and walks on round you. From then on there is always a twist of salt on the cairn at the top of the pass.

fail.log: {npc} drops everything and runs back the way {he} came. You are left with a back-load of salt on the road. You lick it. It is horrible. You are thirsty for three days.

choices.text: Take {him}. A lone human in the dark is what the pass is for

effects.npcDie: taken by the tiger of the pass, alone after dark
effects.log: The gong goes quiet at the bend. In the morning the ten find the salt spilled across the road like frost. Behind you, all the next night, a thin voice sings to the mountain, badly, that it is only a peddler.

events.text: A child crosses the pass at midnight with a twist of paper held in both hands: medicine from the apothecary in the market town for a father with a fever. The child is crying without any sound, the way children cry when there is nobody to hear, and takes the wrong fork at the cairn, the one that goes up to the cliffs.

choices.text: Lie across the wrong fork, so the only way on is the right one

effects.log: The child sees a striped wall where the path was, stands frozen, then backs away and takes the other fork, faster than any child has ever walked. The medicine is home before cockcrow.

choices.text: Walk beside the child, unseen, all the way down

ok.log: You keep to the dark beside the path. Twice the child stops and says, "Who is there?" and twice the forest says nothing. At the village gate the child turns and bows to the dark, just in case.

fail.log: A stick cracks under your paw. The child runs the rest of the way and drops the medicine in the ditch and has to go back for it. It gets home. Your heart, oddly, is still pounding.

choices.text: Leave the child to find the way. Humans must learn their own mountains

effects.log: The child finds the cliff, and turns back, and finds the right fork in the end. It takes all night. In the morning you are not sure whether you taught something or only watched.

events.text: Five men have set up at the bend with sabres and a rope across the road to rob the salt carriers. You hear their leader laughing at the inn: the tiger of the pass is a story the innkeeper tells to sell beds. "I have crossed a hundred passes," he says. "I have never seen a tiger that was not painted on a gate."

choices.text: Roar once from the dark above the bend

effects.log: You roar once. Four of the five are over the next ridge before the echo stops. The leader stays a little longer, which is brave, and wets himself, which is not.

choices.text: Come down among them at the fire

ok.log: You walk into the firelight and sit down. Nobody moves. Then everybody moves. By morning there are five sabres on the road and no men, and the rope is in the gully.

fail.log: Five sabres in the firelight are four more than you thought. You leave with cuts across your shoulders, and they leave too, which is something. (-22 health)
fail.deathCause: five bandits' sabres at the bend of the pass

choices.text: Take the leader, who does not believe in you

effects.log: He sees a tiger at last, the once. The others scatter. On the pass, for years after, a hoarse voice laughs at the bend at night, and travellers say it is telling them there is no such thing as a tiger.

events.text: Dusk on the pass, as on every evening: the cairn, the bend, the travellers coming up out of the shadow of the valley. Today it is a bride's palanquin going over to the next village, its roof draped with a tiger-striped blanket against evil, four bearers sweating and a go-between talking without a pause.

choices.text: Lie still on the rock and let them pass under you

effects.log: The striped blanket goes under your striped chin. The bride lifts the curtain a finger's width, sees you, and lets it drop again without a sound. A sensible person. You hope the groom deserves it.

choices.text: Walk ahead of them to the cairn, so the road is clear

effects.log: The bearers never see you, but they notice that no wolf, no boar and no bandit troubles them, and the go-between takes the credit and doubles the fee.

choices.text: Yawn, loudly, from the dark

effects.log: The bearers cross the top of the pass at a run. The bride arrives early and slightly seasick. The go-between does not talk for the rest of the day, which the whole village counts as an omen.

events.text: The one you took has not gone. It walks ahead of you on the pass at dusk, a little above the ground, barefoot: it has taken off its own straw sandals and set them side by side in the road, the way the old stories say a tiger's ghost does, so the next one will stop to look at them. And it calls. Not its own name. Other names, in a mother's voice, up and down the valley, until somebody in a house below answers.

choices.text: Listen to it, all night

effects.log: You listen. Under the borrowed voices there is a small voice of its own, saying the same thing over and over: it is cold, it wants to go home, somebody else has to come and take its place.

choices.text: Snarl until it falls silent

effects.log: It falls silent. It does not go away. It walks ahead of you without a sound now, which is worse.

choices.text: Follow where it leads

effects.log: It leads you to the shrine at the top of the pass, where a traveller is asleep under the eaves with a bundle for a pillow. It looks back at you, waiting, the way a dog waits for praise.

events.text: A ghost on your pass that is not yours. A charcoal burner, by the smell of it, pine tar and smoke still in the hair, though there is nothing left of the rest. One of your littermates took this one, years ago, on the next mountain, and it has wandered looking for its master ever since. It finds you instead. It bows. "Master," it says, in a voice like a door in the wind. "I have brought you one." There is a traveller asleep in the shrine.

choices.text: "I serve the mountain, not the dead." Send it away

effects.log: It does not understand. It bows again and goes back to the shrine to wait. Ghosts are patient; it is the only thing they have left.

choices.text: Wake the traveller with a growl, so they run before anything happens

effects.log: The traveller runs down the far side of the pass in a nightshirt, carrying one shoe. The ghost watches its gift go with a terrible, polite disappointment.

choices.text: Take the gift

effects.log: The charcoal burner's ghost is free; you see it go up like smoke from a kiln, thanking you. The traveller's ghost is not. It stands in the shrine doorway in the morning, looking at you, learning what it is.

events.text: The ghost explains the rule, in whatever voices it has. A ghost of the tiger goes free only when someone takes its place. It has chosen already: an old herb-gatherer who climbs to the same cliff every morning for bellflower root, alone, singing. It will call from the cliff edge, in the voice of the old one's dead husband, and the old one will go to the edge. All you have to do is wait below.

choices.text: Wait below the cliff

effects.log: A voice at the cliff edge; an old woman who goes to it. Your first ghost goes up into the morning, free, without looking back. Your new one stands at the cliff edge with a basket of bellflower root, and does not understand yet.

choices.text: Lie across the cliff path every morning until the herb-gatherer stops coming

effects.log: A month of mornings in the frost on a narrow path. The herb-gatherer sees a tiger on the path, goes home, and in the end digs root on the other side of the valley. The ghost sulks at the cliff for a year. (-8 health)

choices.text: Ask it its own name

effects.log: It has to think for a long time. A ghost uses so many voices that its own gets lost. In the end it says a name, a plain one, and the name of a village three valleys west, and then, as if surprised: "My mother still puts out a bowl for me."

events.text: Three valleys west, a village of eleven houses. At the end of the lane, on the wall of a house with a sagging thatch, a bowl of rice sits under a cloth, as it has every evening for years. An old woman comes out at dusk to change it. Your ghost stands at the gate and cannot go in.

choices.text: Go in first, in the dark, and lie down by the wall, so the ghost can follow

ok.log: The old woman comes out with the new bowl and sees a tiger lying by her wall. She does not scream. She says her son's name, once, and something behind you answers, and goes past you into the yard, and is gone. The bowl is empty in the morning, for the first time.

fail.log: The dogs find you first. The whole village is out with torches and gongs, and the ghost runs back to the pass ahead of you, terrified of its own home. (-8 health)

choices.text: Leave it at the gate. It must choose to go in

effects.log: It stands at the gate all night. At dawn it turns and follows you back to the pass. Not yet, then. You find that you understand.

events.text: The dead you carry walk ahead of you on the pass at dusk, calling. A mother's voice, a child's, an old man coughing. Down at the inns the travellers hear it and will not cross, and somebody has sent to the county town for the tiger-catchers.

choices.text: Roar them quiet

effects.log: They go quiet for a month. So does every hen in both valleys. The travellers cross again, in tens, with gongs.

choices.text: Lie down across the road between them and the inns, all night

effects.log: The ghosts cannot walk through you. They stand behind you calling, all night, into your back. In the morning you are colder than the snow. (-6 health)

choices.text: Let them call, and see who comes

effects.log: Nobody comes but the tiger-catchers' scout, who listens for an hour from the inn yard, writes something down, and leaves before dark.

events.text: Years on the pass now, and you understand what a ghost is. It is not a punishment. It is a weight. Every one of them hangs on one end of something inside you, and that end goes down a little every year, toward the cold side, the hard side, whether you want it to or not.

choices.text: Swear on the cairn: never another

effects.log: You put your paw on the cairn at the top of the pass where the travellers spit for luck. It is not a human oath; you have no words yet. But the mountain hears it, and so, a long way above the snow, does an old man.

choices.text: Accept it. A tiger eats, and a tiger carries what it eats

effects.log: You stop fighting the weight and let it settle. It is easier to walk like this. That is exactly what frightens you about it.

events.text: The villagers come up the mountain to the place where your ghost's body fell. They burn what is left of it, there, where it lay, and put the ashes in a small box, and leave the box on the spot. They pile stones over it, a hand at a time. On top they turn over an earthenware rice-steamer, the kind with holes in the bottom, and an old man drives the iron spindle from a spinning wheel down through the middle hole with a stone. Then they back away without turning round. Your ghost, standing beside you in the pines, begins to walk toward the cairn.

choices.text: Let it be done

effects.log: It goes into the stones as if into a house. You hear it inside the pot, walking. Round, and round, and round the spindle, like thread. It will be quiet for ever now. It will never be anywhere else.

choices.text: Scatter the villagers before the spindle goes in: it is yours

effects.log: Torches everywhere, a dropped pot, a broken spindle, everybody running. Your ghost comes back to your side and stands very close. You are not sure which of the two of you that was for.

choices.text: Lie in the pines until dawn and listen

effects.log: All night you hear it inside the pot, going round. Round the iron. Round the lightning, as the shamans say. By dawn you have learned how a village lays a tiger's ghost, and you will never quite forgive it, or yourself.

events.text: The cairn on the slope has a shaman now, twice a year: a woman in a red-and-blue robe with a fan and a bell, who dances on the flat ground below the stones and sings to the thing inside the pot, telling it to stay. The village children say there are nine holes in a steamer and the iron is the lightning in the middle one. Inside, the ghost still circles. You can hear it when the wind drops.

choices.text: Knock the spindle out one night and let the ghost go up, not back

ok.log: The iron rings on the stones. Something goes up out of the steamer holes like steam, thin and fast, and does not come to you. It goes up. The shaman finds the spindle in the morning, looks up the mountain for a long time, and does not put it back.

fail.log: The spindle comes out and the ghost comes out with it, straight to your side, glad to see you. It was not ready for the sky. It is yours again.

choices.text: Leave it. The village made its peace in its own way

effects.log: You leave the cairn to the shaman and the circling. Some things that are not justice are still peace.

events.text: Another ghost behind you, and this time you know how it is done. The villagers can only build a cairn where they find the place. You still have the sandals the ghost set side by side in the road.

choices.text: Carry a sandal to the village gate and leave it there, so they come looking

effects.log: They follow the trail of the sandal to the place, and burn, and pile, and turn the pot over, and drive the iron in. Your ghost goes in. The village knows exactly which tiger did it, and now it knows the tiger wanted it found.

choices.text: Find its family instead, however far

ok.log: A whole season of walking and smelling and waiting at gates. In the end, in a fishing village by the sea, an old man comes out to mend a net and the ghost goes past you into the house as if it had only been out for the evening.

fail.log: A season of walking and you never find the house. The ghost follows you back to the pass, tired, and so do you. (-8 health)

events.text: The cairn is old. Moss on the stones, the steamer cracked, the iron spindle rusted to a red thread. Children dare each other to run up and touch the pot. One old woman still comes every spring with a cup of rice liquor, pours it on the stones, and sits for a while. She is the mother. She has always been the mother.

choices.text: Come out of the pines and sit down a little way off

effects.log: She sees you. She does not run; she is past running. The two of you sit by the cairn of her son until the sun goes behind the ridge. Then she gets up and bows, to the stones or to you, and goes down. She comes every spring after that, and you come too.

choices.text: Stay in the pines, out of her sight

effects.log: You watch her pour the liquor, and sit, and go. It is not yours to sit with her. You are fairly sure of that. You are not completely sure.

events.text: A woodcutter, {npc}, comes round a rock and finds you on the path, close enough to touch. You can smell the exact moment {he} decides {he} is dead. Then {npc} throws down the A-frame and falls on {his} face in the pine needles and wails: "Eldest! My lost eldest! Mother always said you were born in the year of the tiger and went up the mountain and never came home, and Mother said you must have turned into a tiger, and look, look at you, Mother was right! Mother weeps for you every night!"

choices.text: Sit down. Lower your head. Go along with it

mem.note: sat down on the path and spared me

effects.log: You do not know why you do it. Perhaps nobody has ever called you anything but tiger. {npc} weeps on your paw for a while, then goes home very fast, looking back over {his} shoulder at the eldest the whole way.

choices.text: Laugh, as a tiger laughs, and let the liar go

effects.log: A clever lie is worth one woodcutter. {npc} runs. You hear the story at the inn a month later, much improved: in this version the woodcutter wrestled you.

choices.text: Eat the liar. A tiger has no family on two legs

effects.npcDie: eaten by a tiger on the mountain path, calling it brother
effects.log: The ghost behind you afterwards calls you eldest, every night, in a voice that does not understand what happened.

events.text: You have been thinking about it. A family, on two legs, in a house with a smoking chimney at the edge of the village: {npc} and an old mother who is half blind and weeps every night for a child who went up the mountain. One night you carry a young boar down to the gate and leave it there.

choices.text: Bring something every month

effects.log: A boar at the new moon, a roe deer at the next. {npc} drags them in before dawn and tells the old mother the eldest sent them. The old mother cries over the meat and cooks it with garlic and gives the best piece to the spirit shelf.

choices.text: Let the old mother see you, once, from the end of the yard

effects.log: The old mother comes out with a lamp and holds it up, and you sit in the edge of the light. Old eyes cannot see much. They see enough. "You got so big," the old mother says. "Do you eat properly up there?"

choices.text: Leave the one boar, and go back to being a tiger

effects.log: The boar feeds them all winter. {npc} goes up the mountain every so often and calls "Eldest!" into the trees. You do not answer, but you listen.

events.text: The village has noticed. A deer at {npc}'s gate every new moon, never a mark on the gate, never a dog barking. The headman asks {npc} for the secret. The neighbours whisper about a fox wife or a buried treasure. A geomancer says the family's ancestral grave must be on a vein of the mountain, and offers to buy the plot.

choices.text: Keep on. Let them whisper

effects.log: {npc} tells everyone it is the ancestors. In a way it is: it is the eldest. The geomancer goes away with nothing but a theory.

choices.text: Leave a hare at the jealous neighbour's gate too

effects.log: The neighbour finds the hare and stops whispering at once. By spring three houses in the village get the odd hare, and the village decides the mountain is generally in a good mood.

choices.text: Stop for a season, until the talk dies

effects.log: A lean season at the gate. {npc} does not complain. In autumn the deer come back and nobody remarks on it; the village has found something else to talk about.

events.text: {npc} comes up the mountain with a bundle and sits on a rock near your den and talks. About when the two of you were small. How you stole the persimmons from the neighbour's tree; how you carried {him} on your back across the flooded stream. None of it happened. {npc} unwraps the bundle: a quilted jacket, old, mended, too small for anything. "Mother kept it. Yours. From before." {npc} believes it now. You can smell that {he} believes it.

choices.text: Lie down near the rock and listen to all of it

effects.log: You listen until dark to a childhood you never had. It is a good one. By the end you would almost swear to the persimmons.

choices.text: Put your nose in the jacket, and keep it in the den

effects.log: It smells of a human child who died a long time ago, of rice and woodsmoke and an old woman's hands. You sleep on it all winter.

choices.text: Roar, so {he} remembers what you are

effects.log: {npc} drops the jacket and goes down the mountain white-faced. Next new moon there is still a deer at the gate, because you are not as hard as your roar. {npc} cries over it.

events.text: {npc} brings a bride up the mountain path in a borrowed red jacket, holding hands, both of them shaking, to bow to the eldest before the ceremony, because the old mother insists a family does things properly. The bride has heard all about you and has not believed a word.

choices.text: Come out of the trees and accept the bow

effects.log: The bride sees you and believes every word at once. Both of them bow twice, to the ground, in the pine needles. You lower your head. It is the strangest wedding in the history of the valley, and the happiest.

choices.text: Leave a pheasant on the path for the feast, and stay hidden

effects.log: They find the pheasant on the path, still warm. The bride stops arguing. The old mother cooks it for the feast and tells every guest it is from the eldest, and the guests nod politely, and eat it very fast.

events.text: Winter. The old mother is ill, and {npc} comes up the mountain in the snow, calling. "Mother wants to see the eldest. Just once, properly. Mother says there will be no going until then." Down in the village there are tiger-catchers at the inn this winter, and the yard of a house is a very small place for a tiger.

choices.text: Go down at midnight, into the yard, and put your head under the old hand

effects.log: The old mother is sitting up in the warm room with the door open to the snow. You put your head through the door. The old hand is very light. "There you are," the old mother says, as if you had been out late. The old mother gets better. Nobody can explain it. There are a good many years left after that, and you feed every one of them.

choices.text: Lie on the ridge above the village and call down to the house, once, softly

effects.log: The whole village hears a tiger call from the ridge at midnight, low, almost gentle. The tiger-catchers sleep through it. The old mother does not, and smiles, and goes to sleep, and in the morning is better.

choices.text: Stay away. It is too dangerous for all of them

effects.log: {npc} waits in the snow until dark and goes home alone. The old mother recovers anyway, and does not reproach you, and a deer still goes to the gate every new moon. But the eldest did not come.

events.text: A notice has gone up on the gate of the county office: a tiger on the mountain, a bounty from the court. Then they come. Twenty of the tiger-catching soldiers in padded armour, with spears, two matchlocks, a crane-skin pouch of shot, beaters with gongs, and a captain, {npc}, who has a ledger in {his} sleeve. They make camp at the shrine at the foot of your mountain. The court pays by the size of the tiger, large, middle or small, and by who strikes it first.

choices.text: Watch them from the bamboo for a month

effects.log: You learn their fires, their watches, their dogs. You learn that {npc} sleeps little and writes a great deal. You learn that the two men with the matchlock need one to hold it and one to fire it.

choices.text: Roar at their camp, the first night

effects.log: Twenty men grab twenty spears. {npc} does not. {npc} listens to the echo with {his} head on one side, and writes down which ridge it came from.

choices.text: Leave the mountain for a season and let them hunt nothing

effects.log: You spend a hungry season two mountains away. They beat every gully on your mountain and find nothing but a bear, which is not worth as much, and makes its own feelings known.

events.text: {npc} has found your track by the frozen stream and is measuring it with a knotted cord. You lie in the rocks above and listen to them do the sums at the fire. A tiger with a paw like that is the large grade. The first spear in it gets the biggest reward and maybe a rank; the second spear less; the third almost nothing. Nobody says what the first spear usually gets from the tiger.

choices.text: Drag a log through your tracks so the print looks twice the size

ok.log: A print the size of a rice-winnowing basket. The men measure it, and measure it again, and argue about who is going to be first spear, and in the end nobody wants to be.

fail.log: {npc} looks at the print a long time and laughs. "A tiger that drags logs," {npc} says. "Clever. Good. Clever ones are worth more."

choices.text: Walk past their fire in the dark, close enough for the sentry to see you

effects.log: The sentry sees an eye as big as a lamp go by, and in the morning, quietly, two of the beaters walk home.

choices.text: Lead them in circles for a month

ok.log: Up the north gully, round the shoulder, back down the south. By the end of the month the men know your mountain better than their own village and have not once seen your tail.

fail.log: A dog cuts the circle. A spear comes out of the bamboo. You get away, but there is a gash in your flank, and now they have your blood on the snow. (-10 health)

events.text: The drive. Before dawn the beaters spread across the bottom of the mountain and start up it with gongs and drums and shouting, and the whole forest runs uphill ahead of them: deer, boar, foxes, a bear. Above, on the saddle, the spearmen wait in a line, and the matchlocks are already smoking, and in the gullies the pit-keeper's covered pits are open.

choices.text: Turn and go back down through the beaters

ok.log: You come down through the line of gongs like a landslide. Nobody is brave enough to be first spear. By noon the beaters are home, and the mountain belongs to you again.

fail.log: A spear in the shoulder from a beater who was braver than the others. You get through, bleeding, and lie up for a month in a cave that smells of bear. (-28 health)
fail.deathCause: the tiger-catchers' drive, a spear from the beaters' line

choices.text: Slip sideways through the bamboo, along the line of the pits

ok.log: You walk the narrow ground between two covered pits, where nobody would think a tiger would walk, and come out behind the spearmen while they are still staring down the hill.

fail.log: The ground goes out from under one hind leg. You claw out of the pit with a stake through the pad. (-15 health)

choices.text: Go to ground in the rock cleft above the spring and wait

effects.log: Three days in a crack of rock with the gongs going past above and below. They do not find you. They find your smell everywhere, and so they will come back.

events.text: A fire in the snow, late, and four of the soldiers around it, and you lying fifty paces off, listening. Three of them are doing the sums. A large tiger is worth so much, but a beater is worth nothing and a dead soldier's widow gets a sack of rice. They have done this for eleven years. They are going home. The fourth one says nothing. The fourth one is {npc}.

choices.text: Let the three go down the mountain unharmed

effects.log: They go at first light with their spears over their shoulders like hoes. One of them looks back at the mountain and says, "Good luck to you, big one," to nobody. You hear it.

choices.text: Follow the three until they are off your mountain, so the fourth is alone

effects.log: You see them off your mountain. When you come back, {npc} is sitting by the dead fire with a spear across {his} knees, waiting. {npc} knew you would.

events.text: {npc} and you, on the snow of the saddle at dawn. No beaters, no gongs, no matchlocks. One spear and a captain who has stopped doing sums. "First spear," {npc} says to you, quite politely. "And no second."

choices.text: Fight to the death

ok.npcDie: killed on the saddle by the tiger of the mountain
ok.log: It is short. The spear goes past your ear. You do not miss. Afterwards there is a new ghost on your mountain that does sums under its breath and will not stop.

fail.log: The spear goes in under the shoulder. You break the shaft and go over the edge of the saddle into the snow, and the captain does not follow. (-32 health)
fail.deathCause: the first spear of a tiger-catching captain

choices.text: Fight, and spare {him} at the end

mem.note: had me down in the snow and let me up

ok.log: You put {npc} on the snow with one paw and hold {him} there, and then you take your paw away. {npc} lies looking at the sky for a long time. When {npc} gets up, the spear stays where it fell.

fail.log: You try to fight without killing and nearly die of it. You both limp off the saddle in opposite directions. (-20 health)

choices.text: Turn your back and walk away into the snow

effects.log: You turn your back on a captain with a spear. Behind you there is a long silence. The spear does not come. When you look back from the treeline, {npc} is sitting in the snow with both hands over {his} face.

events.text: {npc} comes up to the shrine at the foot of your mountain, old now, unarmed, with a jar of rice liquor. {npc} pours a cup on the ground and talks to the mountain. "Do you know where the pelts go? The magistrate sends one to the capital and sells three. The bounty is paid on tigers that never ate anyone, and the man-eaters in the north valley are left alone, because they are dangerous and the pay is the same. I spent my life on it."

choices.text: Lie down where {he} can see you, and listen to the end

effects.log: {npc} talks until the jar is empty: names, ledgers, a magistrate's nephew who buys pelts. You will remember every name. A day will come, a long way up, when the old man of the mountain asks you to break that bounty.

choices.text: Leave a deer at the shrine for {him}

effects.log: {npc} finds the deer, laughs until {he} has to sit down, and eats well for a month. The story goes round the inns: the tiger paid the tiger-catcher.

events.text: Gongs in the valley again. Somebody has posted the bounty, and a new band of tiger-catchers is beating up the lower slopes with dogs, more for the court's rice than for any tiger they expect to find.

choices.text: Leave them a fresh kill at the bottom of the mountain and go up

effects.log: They find a deer, half eaten, and decide the tiger has gone east. You hear them argue at the inn about who saw it first.

choices.text: Shadow them in the bamboo until they lose their nerve

ok.log: A rustle behind the last man, always the last man. By the third day nobody will walk last, and the drive falls apart at the first gully.

fail.log: A dog finds you and the line closes. You get out over a cliff a dog cannot climb. (-12 health)

choices.text: Roar them off the mountain

effects.log: They go. They also go straight to the county office and ask for more men.

events.text: {npc} is sitting on the stone at the top of your pass, the one who put a hand in a tiger's mouth long ago and pulled the bone out of your throat. Older now; a scholar's gat with a split brim, a robe washed thin. {He} has failed the state examination for the third time. The brushes are broken in {his} lap. {He} is not crying. That is what worries you.

choices.text: Come out of the trees and lie down beside {him}

mem.note: lay down beside me after I saved you

effects.log: {npc} looks at you without any surprise at all. "Oh," {npc} says. "It is you." And then {he} cries, at last, into your shoulder, for an hour.

choices.text: Leave a deer on the road below, for the journey home

effects.log: A whole roe deer on the road. {npc} looks at it, then at the mountain, and laughs for the first time in a year. A scholar with no money and a whole deer is suddenly very popular at the inn.

choices.text: Watch from the pines and think about debts

effects.log: A tiger owes a life to a human. A tiger cannot pass an examination. You lie there until dark, thinking, and the thought you end up with is a dangerous one.

events.text: The thought: a tiger in the market of the county town on market day, among the salt and cloth and pots; screaming, stalls going over; and one scholar with a carrying pole who stands in its way and drives it out of the town. The magistrate would have to reward that. The whole province would hear of it. All you have to do is be driven.

choices.text: Do it. Go down into the market

mem.note: made me a hero in the market

ok.log: Pots, screams, a pig loose, and {npc} in the middle of the road with a carrying pole, white as rice, shouting. You let the pole hit your nose, twice, very gently, and you run. By evening {npc} is a hero; by the next spring {npc} has a post at the county office.

fail.log: There is a garrison archer in the market whom nobody told about the plan. You get out over the wall with an arrow in the haunch, and {npc} gets nothing but a story nobody believes. (-16 health)

choices.text: Ask {npc} first. A debt paid without asking is a gift with teeth

effects.log: You cannot speak yet, so you show {npc}: the market, the pole, your nose. It takes all afternoon. In the end {npc} understands, and goes pale, and says, "No. I will sit it a fourth time." And {npc} does.

choices.text: Refuse the thought. A tiger does not play at being a tiger

effects.log: You go back up the mountain. The debt stays where it is, a weight like a bone in the throat. Some debts are like that.

events.text: {npc} comes up to the shrine at the foot of the mountain in a clerk's blue robe, with a servant carrying a whole pig's head on a tray, and makes a proper offering to the mountain spirit, very formal, very correct. Then {npc} sends the servant away and sits on the shrine step and says to the trees: "They give me ledgers to sign that I know are false. If I do not sign, they will find out about the market."

choices.text: Show yourself at the shrine, so {he} remembers who owes whom

effects.log: {npc} looks at you a long time. Then {npc} goes down the mountain and does not sign. Somebody at the county office has a very bad week, and it is not the clerk who walked in with a tiger's look on {his} face.

choices.text: Eat the pig's head and leave {him} to {his} own choices

effects.log: It is an excellent pig's head. {npc} comes back the next month and the shrine is clean, and {npc} understands that a debt, once paid, is paid. What {npc} signs after that is between {him} and heaven.

events.text: {npc} is old, and sick, and has walked up the pass one last time to sit on the same stone. "I dreamed of you," {npc} says, "in the shape of a woman in a white jacket, who offered to die so that I could have my rank. In the dream I said yes. I woke up ashamed. A man should not be paid twice for one bone."

choices.text: Lie down with your head against {his} knee until the sun goes

effects.npcPass: old age, on the stone at the top of the pass
effects.log: {npc} puts a hand on your head, the same hand that went into your mouth. When the sun goes behind the ridge the hand stops moving. You stay until morning, and carry the gat down to the village gate, so they will know where to look.

choices.text: Bring {him} home on your back, down the mountain in the dark

effects.npcPass: old age, at home, a night after the tiger carried the old scholar down
effects.log: A whole village sees a tiger walk up its lane at midnight with an old scholar asleep on its back, and set the scholar down at the right gate, and go. Nobody in that village will ever hurt a tiger again.

events.text: The oldest trouble on a pass: men who would rather take than carry. A band of a dozen has moved into the ravine below the bend, with a lookout on the rock and a tethered ox that is not theirs. Twice this month the salt carriers have come down the far side with nothing.

choices.text: Take the ox out of the middle of their camp at night

ok.log: In the morning there is a rope and no ox and a pug mark as big as a winnowing basket in the ash of the fire. The lookout is not on the rock the next night. Nor is anybody else.

fail.log: The ox bellows, the camp wakes, and twelve men with torches and sabres chase you up the ravine. You get the ox in the end. You also get a sabre cut. (-12 health)

choices.text: Sit on their lookout rock all day, in plain sight

effects.log: Nobody in the camp can go to relieve themselves all day. By evening they are negotiating with each other about who has to walk past you. By morning they are gone.

choices.text: Leave them. Robbers are a human problem

effects.log: The salt carriers stop coming. The inn at the foot of the pass closes for a season. You learn that a human problem on your pass is your problem too.

events.text: Robbers at the bend again, another band, another season: a family's cart turned over, a man held face down on the road, a woman pleading for the seed rice.

choices.text: Come down the slope like a falling rock

ok.log: The robbers leave everything, including two sabres and one shoe. The family picks up the seed rice grain by grain, bowing to the slope you came down.

fail.log: One of them is a soldier once and keeps his head. You drive them off with a spear-cut along your ribs. (-14 health)

choices.text: Roar from the ridge

effects.log: Robbers and family run in opposite directions. The family comes back for the cart. The robbers do not come back at all.

choices.text: Take one of the robbers

effects.log: The family sees a robber taken off the road into the dark, and runs. They tell the village the tiger of the pass is just. The ghost behind you does not agree.

events.text: The bandit chief comes up the ravine alone at dusk with a whole leg of beef on his shoulder and drops it on the flat rock below your den. "An arrangement," he says, to the dark. "Meat every new moon. You keep the pass empty of soldiers and do not come into the ravine. Everybody eats."

choices.text: Eat the meat and keep the bargain

effects.log: Meat every new moon. The pass is full of robbers and empty of soldiers. The travellers learn to go round by the long road. The magpie will not speak to you.

choices.text: Eat the meat, and come into the ravine anyway

effects.log: He did say everybody eats. The band leaves before the next new moon, and the chief tells everyone in the next province that tigers have no honour, which is rich.

choices.text: Push the meat back off the rock with one paw

effects.log: The leg of beef rolls down the ravine at his feet. He looks at it for a long time. "Your loss," he says, and picks it up, and you see his hands are shaking.

events.text: The Autumn Court. The magpie has brought you a case under Turtle Beak, the mansion of soldiers: the robbers in the ravine have been caught by the villagers and tied to the pines below the shrine, and they are not robbers. They are deserters from the border fort, nine of them. Their commander sold their winter rations and their quilted coats to a merchant and told them to eat bark. Two men died of cold before the rest walked away. On the road, hungry, they robbed. One of them killed a carter who fought back.

choices.text: Punish the one who killed. Pardon the eight. Send the magpie to the fort about the commander

effects.log: The killer goes to the county with his hands tied. Eight hungry men go home to their villages. That winter the commander of the border fort wakes to find a tiger's paw print on the floor of his storeroom, beside the empty ration sacks, and writes to the governor in his own hand. The magpie files the case under Turtle Beak. It was just.

choices.text: Punish all nine. A deserter is a deserter

effects.log: Nine men go to the county with their hands tied, and the commander who sold their coats sends a letter thanking the magistrate. The magpie writes it down and does not file it anywhere.

choices.text: Pardon all nine. Hunger is not a crime

effects.log: All nine go free, the killer with them. A carter's widow in the next valley is told the tiger let them go. The magpie writes it down and does not file it anywhere.

events.text: Scent on your trees that is not yours: higher up the bark than you can reach, and older, and colder, a smell of the forests beyond the great river in the north where the snow lies half the year. Something bigger than you has walked your bounds in the night, and left its own mark over every one of yours.

choices.text: Mark over every one of its marks, higher, the same night

effects.log: You stand on your hind legs against every tree it marked and scratch above its scratches until your claws bleed. In the morning, two lines of marks on every tree: the mountain is having an argument.

choices.text: Track it, and see it before it sees you

ok.log: You find it asleep in the sun on the north slope: half again your size, a coat almost black at the stripes, an old scar across the muzzle from a spear. It is not stupid. It is only hungry, and far from home.

fail.log: It sees you first. It does not attack. It only looks at you across a gully, and then it yawns. (-6 health, mostly pride)

events.text: The tiger from the north has killed a boar on your side of the ridge, eaten the best of it and left the head on your flat rock, facing your den, tusks up.

choices.text: Eat the head, in plain sight of the north slope

effects.log: You crack the skull on your rock where it can hear. Insult for insult. That night it roars from the north slope for an hour, and the villages below bar every door.

choices.text: Push the head off the rock and leave it for the crows

effects.log: You do not take the bait. The crows do. It watches you not take it, and you hope it is worried.

choices.text: Go to the north slope and leave a boar of your own, head up, on its rock

ok.log: It takes you all night to drag a whole boar up the north slope. In the morning there is a boar on its rock and a tiger from the north staring at it as if it had been slapped.

fail.log: You get the boar halfway up the slope and it catches you there, dragging. The fight is short and nobody wins. (-10 health)

events.text: Dawn on the ridge, snow falling slowly. It is waiting at the top, where the old boundary pine is split by lightning. Half again your size. You can hear the villagers below banging pots at the sound of two tigers breathing.

choices.text: Fight it for the mountain

ok.log: It is bigger. You are home. You know where the ice is under the snow on the ridge, and it does not, and when it slips you are on its back. It runs, and it does not come back. The mountain is yours.

fail.log: It throws you off the ridge into the birches. You lie there until noon, and when you climb back up, its marks are on the split pine. (-32 health)
fail.deathCause: the tiger from the north, on the ridge at dawn

choices.text: Lead it onto the ice of the high tarn

ok.log: You run, and it follows, out across the snow that hides the frozen tarn. You know where the ice is thin. It does not. It goes through, and claws out, and goes north dripping, and the whole mountain hears it go. The mountain is yours.

fail.log: It does not follow you onto the ice. It sits on the shore and waits for you to come off. You come off cold, and lose. (-16 health)

choices.text: Give it the north slope, and keep the south

effects.log: You walk away from the split pine. It lets you. A mountain with two tigers is a hungry mountain, and both of you know it; this is not over. (Mark the Bounds to hold the mountain.)

events.text: Years after, in the gully below the north slope, you find it again: the tiger from the north, very old now, grey at the muzzle, one eye white. It has come back to your mountain to lie down. It looks at you and does not get up.

choices.text: Let it die here in peace, and keep the crows off

effects.log: You lie at the top of the gully for nine days. On the tenth it is gone, and you bury nothing, because tigers do not, but you keep the crows off until the snow does it for you.

choices.text: Drive it off. This is your mountain

effects.log: It gets up, slowly, and walks north. It does not make it to the river. You find out from the magpie, later, and you are not sure what you feel.

events.text: A new king has taken the city on the plain below the western mountains, and his ministers say it is not a capital while tigers walk on the hills above the palace. So the king has prayed to the mountain gods, and the mountain gods have agreed: every tiger on the hills goes north, across the great river, by the first snow. The magpie brings the order. You are to lead them. In a cleft on the hill behind the city lies a tigress, heavy with cubs, who cannot walk that far and says so.

choices.text: Lead them all north, the tigress too, slowly

effects.log: Forty tigers on the move, at the pace of the heaviest one. You carry nothing and you carry all of it. The tigress walks at the back and does not speak to you for the whole road.

choices.text: Hide the tigress in the rocks above the city and lead the rest

effects.log: You find her a cleft under a rock shaped like a crouching tiger, which seems only fair, and cover the trail. Then you lead thirty-nine tigers north and tell the magpie there were thirty-nine.

choices.text: Go to the old man of the mountain and ask that one may stay

ok.log: He listens, pulling his beard. "One," he says. "One. And when her cubs fill the hill, the king can pray to me again." You lead the rest north. She stays, and is very rude about it.

fail.log: "A king asked," he says. "Kings are rare enough. Go." You lead all of them north, the tigress at the back.

events.text: The great river at the first snow: ice from bank to bank, groaning. On the far side, the northern forests, dark and endless. Forty tigers do not like ice. One cub, born on the road, goes through a black patch near the middle.

choices.text: Go in after it

ok.log: You go through the ice and come up with the cub in your teeth. Forty tigers watch you climb out. After that, on the far bank, every one of them lowers its head to you before it goes into the trees.

fail.log: The cold closes over you. You get out. The cub does not. The tigers go into the northern trees one by one, without looking back. (-20 health)

choices.text: Lie down on the ice to spread it, and let the others pull the cub out

effects.log: You lie flat over the black patch, the ice bending under you, while the cub's mother hooks it out by the scruff. Nobody thanks you. Tigers do not. Nobody forgets either.

events.text: Twenty years on, the hill above the king's city is full of tigers again, all of them the tigress's grandchildren. Woodcutters cross the pass behind the hill only in tens, and gather at the inn below it until they are ten, and people say that no tiger in the land does not know that hill. The king's grandson has asked the mountain gods again.

choices.text: Go and speak for them to the old man

effects.log: "They eat a woodcutter now and then," the old man says. "They eat fewer than the king's soldiers do." He does not send them north. The city learns to live under its tigers, and comes to boast of them.

choices.text: Lead the grandchildren north yourself, as you should have the first time

effects.log: The hill is empty by spring. The city is very proud of itself. On the far side of the great river an old tigress, hearing who has come, refuses to see you.

events.text: A tiger comes south over the great river at midwinter and up to your mountain: big, dark at the stripes, hungry, born in the northern forests to one of the tigers you led there. It knows your smell. Its mother told it, it says, who made them leave.

choices.text: Let it have a valley at the edge of your bounds

effects.log: It takes the valley, warily. It turns out to be a good neighbour, and later, when hunters come, a useful one.

choices.text: Drive it back across the river

ok.log: It goes back over the ice. From the far bank it looks at you for a long time. Exile, it turns out, is a thing that can be done twice.

fail.log: It is young and it has been angry its whole life. You both bleed on the snow, and it takes the valley anyway. (-18 health)

choices.text: Tell it the truth: you led them because you were told to

effects.log: It listens. "And if you are told again?" it asks. You have no answer. It goes back north, which is somehow worse than a fight.

events.text: Up on the high saddle between two peaks, where the wind never stops, there is a snowdrift that breathes. Your grandmother: older than any tiger you have smelled, so big that the snow settles on her back like on a rock, and without a single tooth left in her head. Other tigers bring her what she can eat. You bring her a deer's liver. She mumbles it for an hour, and then looks at you with eyes like old ice and says: "A tiger who never forgives is a trap. A tiger who always forgives is a rug."

choices.text: Ask her what you are meant to be, then

effects.log: "Level," she says. "A beam with a stone on each end. You will spend your whole life with your paw on it, and you will never once be allowed to take it off." Then she goes to sleep.

choices.text: Bring her another liver, and another, all winter

effects.log: All winter you climb to the saddle with something soft. She never thanks you. In spring she tells you, without looking up, that you hunt like your grandfather, and you understand that is the highest praise she has.

choices.text: Tell her you are no rug

effects.log: "Good," she says. "Now go away and find out whether you are a trap." She laughs, which with no teeth is a terrible thing to see.

events.text: A fox has been stealing from your grandmother: the soft things the other tigers leave. Today you catch it on the saddle with a hare in its mouth. Your grandmother opens one eye. "Judge it," she says. "I want to watch."

choices.text: Punish it: one swipe, and the fox goes off the saddle

effects.log: "Hm," says your grandmother. "Correct. Too much. The beam went down on that end." The fox limps away and steals from someone else.

choices.text: Pardon it: let it go with the hare

effects.log: "Hm," says your grandmother. "Kind. Too kind. The beam went up on that end." The fox comes back the next night, with friends.

choices.text: Make it bring her a hare every new moon for a year

effects.log: The fox looks at you, at the old tigress, at the long fall off the saddle. It agrees. For a year your grandmother eats very well and the fox becomes extremely good at hares. "That," she says, "was level."

events.text: A long night on the saddle in a blizzard, and your grandmother talks. About the bear and the tiger in the cave with the mugwort and the garlic, and the tiger who left on the twentieth day because it was hungry; that was our family, she says, and we have been hungry ever since. About the four who sit at the corners of the sky: the Black Tortoise with the snake round it in the north, the Vermilion Bird over the southern sea, a blue-green one in the east who is not born yet, and a white one in the west whose seat is empty.

choices.text: "Whose seat?"

effects.log: "Nobody's," she says. "Not yet." She looks at you a long time in the dark. "You eat too much to sit in it," she says, and goes to sleep. You lie awake until the blizzard stops.

choices.text: "Why did our ancestor leave the cave?"

effects.log: "Because it was day twenty and the garlic was finished," she says. "And because outside the cave there was a deer. There is always a deer." She snores. You think about deer for a week.

events.text: Your grandmother is so old now that the snow does not melt on her at all. She has decided, she tells you, not to die yet. "There is a valley I want to see," she says. "Where the left ridge and the right ridge hold it like two hands. The right ridge is waiting for someone. So is the left. I want to see who comes."

choices.text: Promise to carry her there when you find it

effects.log: "Carry," she says. "Ha." But she looks pleased, and for the rest of that winter she gets up every morning, which she had stopped doing.

choices.text: Ask who is coming to the left

effects.log: "Something with no manners," she says. "They never have any, at first. You will have to teach it. Try not to eat it." She seems to find this very funny.

events.text: The hunger is not in your belly any more. It is in your eyes. Below you on the pass at dusk, one lantern, one traveller, alone, an old man with a back-load of dried fish, who keeps stopping to rest. Every time he stops you find you have moved a little closer.

choices.text: Take him

effects.log: It is very quick and you are very full, and in the morning there is dried fish all over the pass and a ghost behind you that keeps asking where its load has gone.

choices.text: Turn your back on the road and go for the bear in its winter den

ok.log: A bear woken in midwinter is the worst-tempered thing on any mountain. It is also the most meat. You come out of the den bloody and full, and the old man with the fish never knows.

fail.log: The bear is not as asleep as you hoped. You get some of it. It gets some of you. (-25 health)
fail.deathCause: a bear woken in its winter den, when hunger had taken your sense

choices.text: Eat the frozen carcass in the gully, whatever it is

effects.log: A deer the wolves left a month ago, frozen and foul. You eat it all. You are sick for three days in the snow, and you are not a man-eater. (-10 health)

events.text: Hunger has walked you down to the edge of the village without your noticing. You are standing in the dark by a byre, with your nose against the gap in the wall. A calf. Beyond it, in the warm room, a family asleep. The dogs have not smelled you yet. The dogs are also meat.

choices.text: The calf

effects.log: In the morning the family finds the wall broken and the calf gone, and the father sits down in the byre and does not get up for a long time. A calf is a year of ploughing. But it is not a person, and there is no ghost.

choices.text: The dogs

effects.log: Two dogs, and the whole village awake with torches and gongs, and you up the slope again. Not enough. Enough for now.

choices.text: Go back up the mountain. Hunt till you drop

ok.log: Up in the high snow at first light, a red deer that has stumbled in a drift. The mountain, sometimes, is kind.

fail.log: Three days of nothing but a hare. You stagger back to the den and sleep like the dead. The village never knows how close it was. (-15 health)

events.text: At the shrine at the foot of the mountain the villagers have left their autumn offering to the mountain spirit: a whole boiled pig's head, rice cakes, a jar of rice liquor, a candle. It is not for you. It is for the old man of the mountain. Your hunger does not care whose it is.

choices.text: Eat it all

effects.log: The villagers find the shrine licked clean and are delighted: the spirit accepted. Somewhere above the snow an old man knows exactly who accepted it, and says nothing, which is worse than saying something.

choices.text: Take only the pig's head, and leave the rest

effects.log: A compromise between your stomach and your manners. Both of them grumble.

choices.text: Leave it, and lie down beside it, and guard it from the foxes

effects.log: All night beside a pig's head, starving, keeping the foxes off. In the morning a cold wind comes down off the summit and pushes half of it across the stone toward you, as if by a careful hand. You do not remember ever being so grateful. (-15 health)

events.text: Your ghost has been out on the pass, calling. It comes back to you at midnight and stands very close and says, in the voice of somebody's mother: "Master, there is one asleep under the shrine eaves. Only one. I have taken off their sandals for you." You can smell the sleeper from here. You can smell nothing else.

choices.text: Go to the shrine

effects.log: Your old ghost goes free with a sigh like a door closing. The new one stands under the shrine eaves in the morning in its bare feet, looking for its sandals.

choices.text: Lie down on top of the ghost's path so it cannot go back

effects.log: The sleeper wakes at dawn, puts on a pair of sandals left neatly by the step, and walks on over the pass, puzzled and alive. You eat a fox, a hare, and some bark. (-15 health)

events.text: The oldest story there is comes back to you in the worst of it: the cave, the mugwort, the garlic, and the tiger who left on the twentieth day because there was a deer outside. You find a cave. You lie down in the dark. You tell yourself you will not go out for twenty days. Then twenty-one.

choices.text: Stay in the dark

ok.log: Day nineteen is the worst. Day twenty you can hear deer outside. Day twenty-one you are still there, and something has broken: the hunger is quiet, like a fever after it turns. You come out thin and calm, and walk past three deer. (-10 health)

fail.log: Day nineteen. There is a deer outside the cave. There is always a deer. You come out like your ancestor did, and eat it, and lie in the snow afterwards, ashamed. (-12 health)

choices.text: Give up the cave and go down to the road

effects.log: You come out on the third day. A carter on the pass road, alone. Your ancestor at least lasted twenty.

events.text: A year with no deer. The snow came early and stayed. In the cave below your den a family has taken shelter from the cold: a grandfather, two parents, three children, a pot with nothing in it. They know whose cave this is. The grandfather comes out alone into the snow at dusk, kneels where you can see him, and says: "Take me. I am old. Let the children be."

choices.text: Take the grandfather, as he asks

effects.log: He does not run. In the spring the family goes down to the village, and the children grow up, and their own children are told of a grandfather who walked out into the snow. The ghost behind you is the quietest you have ever had. It never lures anyone. It only sits.

choices.text: Go down the far side of the mountain to the herds in the next valley

ok.log: Three nights there, three nights back, a herdsman's horse in between. When you come home there is still smoke from the cave, and you leave the hindquarter at its mouth.

fail.log: The herdsmen have dogs and spears. You come back with a lame foreleg and a lamb. The family in the cave eats the lamb. You do not mind as much as you expected. (-20 health)

choices.text: Lie down across the cave mouth and starve with them

effects.log: A tiger lying across a cave mouth all winter keeps out the wind and the wolves. The family lives, just. In spring the children touch your stripes before they go. You live, just. (-25 health)

events.text: The hunger again, at the top of its strength, like a second tiger inside the first. The mountain is very quiet. The road below is not.

choices.text: Hunt a bear

ok.log: A long fight in a ravine. A long meal afterwards. The road below never knows.

fail.log: The bear gets away and leaves you a marmot's worth of meat and a torn ear. (-20 health)

choices.text: Roar from the ridge until the hunger passes

effects.log: You roar all night. Every village in two valleys bars its doors and every traveller stays at the inn. By morning the hunger is a little smaller and your throat is raw. (-10 health)

choices.text: Go down to the road

effects.log: There is a traveller. There is always a traveller. In the morning there is a ghost.

variants: The hunger again. It wakes before you do now, and it is bigger than you are. The deer have gone over the far ridge. On the road below, a lantern is moving.
Another winter, and the old hunger with it, pacing inside you like a tiger in a cage too small. The forest is empty. The road below is not.
The hunger comes back the way the snow does: quietly, and then everywhere. Nothing moves on the mountain. Far below, someone on the road is singing to keep warm.
You have not eaten since the leaves fell, and the hunger is louder than the wind. A bear is sleeping somewhere in these hills. A traveller is walking the pass below. Both of them are food.

events.text: At the very top of your mountain, where no human climbs, under the oldest pine, an old man is sitting on a rock. White beard to his belt, a red robe gone pink with sun, a staff of twisted root. Snow has settled on his shoulders and does not melt. He smells of pine resin and cold stone and nothing at all of human. Two small children in topknots stand behind him, one with a peach, one with a fan, and they are not afraid of you either. "So," says the old man. "You are the one the magpie never shuts up about."
events.arc: The Old Man of the Mountain

choices.text: Lie down at his feet

effects.log: He does not touch you, not yet. He looks at you for a long time, the way a farmer looks at a field before planting. "Hm," he says. "We will see." The children giggle.

choices.text: Circle him, slowly, testing the air

effects.log: He smells of the whole mountain at once: every spring, every den, every grave. You come round the third time and understand that you are walking round the mountain, and that he is letting you.

choices.text: Show your teeth. Nobody sits on your summit

effects.log: The old man laughs until he coughs. "Your summit," he says to the child with the fan. "Did you hear? Its summit." Then he is gone, and the rock is only a rock, and the snow on it is old.

events.text: Under the old pine again, and this time the old man reaches out without a word and puts his hand on your head, between the ears. It is a light, dry, old hand. Through it you feel the mountain all at once: the springs under the stones, the deer asleep in the bracken, every grave, every shrine, every human crossing at dusk. "My tiger," he says. "Now."
events.arc: The Old Man of the Mountain

choices.text: Bow your head under his hand

effects.log: His hand stays on your head until the sun goes down. When he takes it away you are not just a tiger on a mountain any more. You are the mountain's tiger, and it will be some time before you understand the difference.

choices.text: Ask what it will cost

effects.log: "Errands," he says. "Verdicts. And you will not eat anyone I am fond of, which is most of them." He takes his hand away. "And the rest of your life. That is the usual price."

choices.text: Twist away, and then come back

effects.log: You flinch out from under his hand and then stand there, ashamed, and come back and put your head under it yourself. "Good," he says. "A tiger who comes back on its own is worth two who never left."

events.text: The shrine on the pass is a little wooden hall the size of a woodshed, with a plank painting inside: an old man under a pine, two children, and a tiger. The old man is quite good. The tiger looks like a cat that has been told bad news, with a long face and crossed eyes. Every villager who crosses bows to it. It is not quite you yet.
events.arc: The Old Man of the Mountain

choices.text: Lie in the shrine door at dawn, so a villager sees you beside it

effects.log: An old woman with a bundle of rice cakes sees a real tiger lying in front of the painted one, and sets the rice cakes down very carefully, and backs away bowing. By the autumn the shrine has a new roof.

choices.text: Leave a sprig of pine on the offering stone

effects.log: Every morning for a year, a fresh sprig of pine on the stone, and no tracks. The village decides the mountain spirit is pleased. The old man under the pine says nothing, but the snow on his shoulders looks a little lighter.

choices.text: Sit in front of the painting and stare at it until you understand it

effects.log: The painted tiger stares back with crossed eyes. You understand at last: it is not a picture of a tiger. It is a picture of the mountain spirit's power, and the painter had never seen one, and has drawn instead what the villagers feel. That is worse than ridiculous. That is accurate.

events.text: The old man has a small errand for you, not a real one. A sow and her piglets have rooted up the bellflower slope on the east side, and the village women dig there. "Do not eat them," he says. "Move them." A tiger's whole nature is in the way of that sentence.
events.arc: The Old Man of the Mountain

choices.text: Herd the boars over the ridge, slowly, for a whole season

effects.log: Nine piglets, one sow, a season of patience and one bite on your foreleg from the sow, who did not see the point. The women dig bellflower all autumn. The old man nods once. (-6 health)

choices.text: Eat one piglet, and move the rest

effects.log: The rest move fast after that. "I said do not eat them," the old man says. "Them," you think. He hears you think it, and does not quite smile.

choices.text: Ask why the boars matter less than the women

effects.log: "They do not," he says. "The boars have the whole mountain and the women have one slope." You move the boars. It takes you a long time to stop turning that over.

events.text: A temple painter has come up to the pass to repaint the shrine plank, and has sat on the step all morning with a brush in his mouth, sketching the mountain, waiting for the spirit to show him what it looks like. He is still there at dusk. So are you, in the trees.
events.arc: The Old Man of the Mountain

choices.text: Come out and lie down in front of him, quite still, for an hour

effects.log: He does not breathe for an hour. Then he paints faster than you have seen anything move. The new plank goes up in the spring: an old man under a pine, two children, and a tiger that is, unmistakably, you. Somewhere above the snow the old man laughs.

choices.text: Stay in the trees, and let him paint what he imagines

effects.log: He paints a tiger with a long face and crossed eyes. Some things are a tradition. You find, to your surprise, that you do not mind.

events.text: The magpie lands on the pine above your head and will not stop talking. It is the old man's bird, you have learned; it carries what he wants you to know, and a good deal he does not. Today: an ox has been stolen in the lower village, and the wrong man is going to be beaten for it.

choices.text: Go down and find the ox by its smell

ok.log: The ox is in the headman's nephew's back field behind a stack of millet straw. You lie down next to it until somebody notices. The wrong man is not beaten. The right one has a very bad year.

fail.log: You find an ox. It is a different ox. Its owner sees you and decides his ox is not worth it, and the village is in uproar for a month.

choices.text: Tell the magpie it is human business

effects.log: The magpie tells you, at length, that everything on this mountain is your business now. Then it tells the whole forest you said that.

events.text: The magpie again, upside down on a branch, very pleased with itself. News of a hunt: tiger-catchers at the county town, and a magistrate who wants a pelt for the capital before the new year.

choices.text: Go two mountains east for a season

effects.log: The hunters beat your mountain from end to end and find a very old bear. The magistrate sends the bear's pelt to the capital and calls it a striped bear. Nobody in the capital argues.

choices.text: Stay, and leave your marks very high on the trees by the road

effects.log: The hunters see the height of the marks and do the sums. Half of them go home. The other half are more careful, and the magpie finds that very funny.

events.text: The magpie, breathless. News of a birth: in a hut at the edge of the high village, a child born at midnight in the year of the tiger, the hour of the tiger, the month of the tiger. The midwife has fainted. The whole village is waiting to see whether you come.

choices.text: Come and lie at the gate until dawn

effects.log: You lie at the gate in the snow and the village watches you from behind every door. At dawn the father brings the baby to the gate wrapped in a quilt, and holds it up. You look at each other. Then you go. That child will never be afraid of anything as long as it lives.

choices.text: Stay on the ridge and roar once, so the child hears

effects.log: One roar, rolling down the valley at dawn. The baby, the midwife swears, roared back.

choices.text: Do not go. Omens are human business

effects.log: The village is disappointed. The child grows up perfectly ordinary, and is happy, which is rarer than being an omen.

events.text: The magpie comes in the dark, with no jokes at all. In the high village on the north side, a parent is dying of fever, and the only medicine is at the apothecary in the market town on the south side, across the whole mountain. A child has gone for it, alone, tonight, and must be home before dawn or it will not matter. The old man's words, the magpie says, are these: "Carry. Do not frighten. Do not eat."

choices.text: Go at once

effects.log: You go down the south side at a run, through snow to the shoulder, toward a single lantern on the market road coming the other way.

choices.text: Ask the magpie why a tiger, and not a deer, or a horse

effects.log: "Because a deer would get lost and a horse would get eaten," the magpie says, "by you. Go." You go.

choices.text: "A tiger is not a pack-horse"

effects.log: The magpie does not answer. It sits on the branch and looks at you until you get up and go, sulking, toward the lantern on the market road.

events.text: The child is {npc}, nine years old, with a cloth bundle of medicine tied to one wrist so it cannot be dropped, and a lantern that is going out. Halfway up the mountain, in the snow, the lantern goes out. {npc} stands very still in the dark and says, out loud, the way the grandmothers teach: "Mountain spirit, I am only going home. Please." Then {npc} sees your eyes.

choices.text: Lie down in the path and wait for the child to understand

ok.log: A long time. Then a small cold hand on your shoulder, and a small weight on your back, and two fists in your fur. You go over the top of the mountain like a wind. Halfway down {npc} falls asleep, and you go slower so as not to wake the child. At the gate, before dawn, you lie down and the child slides off and runs in with the medicine. The errand is done.

fail.log: {npc} runs. Into the snow, off the path, the wrong way. You spend the night herding a terrified child home by getting in front of it from every other direction. You reach the village after dawn. The parent lives, but not because of you, and the old man knows it.

choices.text: Pick the child up by the jacket collar, like a cub, and run

ok.log: One scream, and then none, because the child is going over the mountain faster than any child ever has and is too astonished to scream. You put {npc} down at the gate before cockcrow, medicine and all. The errand is done, though the old man says, mildly, "Carry, I said. Not fetch."

fail.log: The jacket tears. The child falls in the snow. You both get home at dawn, wet and frightened and late. The parent lives anyway. The errand is not done. (-8 health)

choices.text: Walk ahead, unseen, and be the path

mem.note: walked ahead of me over the mountain

ok.log: You stay just ahead in the dark, breaking the snow, so the easiest way is always the right one. {npc} never sees you, only a trench in the snow that goes exactly where it should. Home before dawn. The errand is done.

fail.log: The snow fills your trench as fast as you make it. {npc} goes astray at the saddle and is found at noon by the villagers. The errand is not done.

events.text: Another winter, another fever, another child on the mountain at night with medicine in a cloth: the old man, it seems, does not give up on an errand just because the tiger failed it. This one is older, eleven, and carrying a sick little brother on one hip as well as the medicine.

choices.text: Lie down in the path and wait

ok.log: You have learned. You lie down and do not look at them, and wait, and let them come to you. Two children on your back over the mountain, one asleep, one holding the medicine in both hands. The errand is done.

fail.log: Not again. They run, the little one howling. You get them home by noon by walking behind them and growling at the wolves, and it is not good enough. (The errand waits.)

choices.text: Take the medicine in your mouth and run it to the village yourself, and come back for them

effects.log: The village wakes to a tiger at the gate with a cloth bundle in its teeth. Then it goes back up the mountain, and comes down again at dawn with two children walking beside it holding its fur. It is not quite what the old man said. He lets it pass.

events.text: {npc}, grown and grey at the temples, climbs the pass with a child of {his} own and stops at the shrine, and tells the child the story: the night the lantern went out, the warm striped back, the smell of snow and pine, waking at the gate. "It went slower when I fell asleep," {npc} says. "I noticed. I never told anyone that part."

choices.text: Come out of the trees, so the child sees you too

effects.log: The child sees you and does not scream, because the child has been told about you since before it could talk. {npc} bows to the ground. You lower your head. The child goes home and tells every child in the village, and none of them believe it, and all of them want it to be true.

choices.text: Stay in the trees and listen to the story to the end

effects.log: It is a good story. It has improved: in this version you are white, and the mountain is twice as high. You do not correct it.

events.text: The old man explains the Autumn Court under the pine, while the leaves come down. Spring is the east's, and it rewards; autumn is the west's, and it judges. Seven stars in the western sky, from Legs to the Three Stars, and every case on earth belongs under one of them: water under Legs, crowds under Bond, granaries under Stomach, raiders and funerals under Hairy Head, hunters under Net, soldiers under Turtle Beak, a life for a life under the Three Stars. "You sit on the flat rock," he says. "The magpie writes. Be just, or be nothing."

choices.text: Accept the seat

effects.log: The flat rock in the maple clearing is cold under you. The magpie lands on the branch beside it, and straightens its tail, and for once does not say a word.

choices.text: "Who judges the judge?"

effects.log: "The three straight stars in the middle," he says, and points west, where they are rising: the Balance. "And the three small ones under them, the Punishment, which judges everyone else." He seems pleased you asked. He does not seem to think it is a comforting answer.

choices.text: "I am a tiger. I eat what I judge"

effects.log: "Then judge very carefully," the old man says, "because you will also carry whatever you eat." He looks at the ghosts behind you, if there are any, or at the place where they would stand.

events.text: The first case comes up the mountain on its own feet: two villages, one ditch. In the drought the upper village dammed the ditch to save its own rice. The lower village's paddies cracked. A man from the lower village broke the dam at night; a man from the upper village caught him; there was a fight; a leg was broken. Now both villages stand in the maple clearing in their best white clothes, shouting at a flat rock with a tiger on it.

choices.text: Hear both, then go and look at the ditch yourself

effects.log: You walk the whole ditch at night from the spring to the last paddy, with the magpie riding on your head complaining. At the fork, half buried in mud, there is an old stone with two names cut in it.

choices.text: Judge now, for the lower village: their rice died

effects.log: The lower village cheers. The upper village goes home muttering, and the next drought it dams the ditch again, higher. The magpie writes it down and files it nowhere.

choices.text: Judge now, for the upper village: they dug the ditch

effects.log: The upper village cheers. The lower village goes home with its broken leg and its cracked paddies. The magpie writes it down and files it nowhere.

events.text: The stone at the fork, cleaned of mud: two family names cut in it a hundred years ago, one above the other, and under them, plain as a ploughed line, "dug together, shared together." The ditch was never the upper village's. Both grandfathers dug it. The upper village has known that for a hundred years and has forgotten it on purpose.

choices.text: Mercy: open the dam by the old stone, half and half; the upper village works the lower one's field until the leg heals

effects.log: Grumbling, both villages dig the stone up and set it at the fork where everyone can see it. The magpie files the case under Legs, the mansion of ditches and drains. It was just. Your first.

choices.text: Severity: the upper headman closed a shared ditch in a drought; the dam-breaker broke a man's leg. Punish both

effects.log: The upper headman sits a month in the village stocks; the dam-breaker pays for the leg in rice. Nobody is happy, which, the old man says, is sometimes how you know. The magpie files the case under Legs. It was just. Your first.

choices.text: Pardon the dam-breaker and leave it at that

effects.log: The dam-breaker goes free; the stone goes back under the mud. Nothing changes. The magpie writes it down, looks at you, and files it nowhere.

events.text: Drought again, and the ditch is dammed again, and higher, and the two villages are in the maple clearing again in their white clothes, and this time there are sickles. Your verdict did not hold. The magpie, on its branch, has the decency not to say so.
