choices.text: Go down to the fork and dig for whatever is under the mud

ok.log: You find the old stone with two names on it: dug together, shared together. You drag it into the clearing in your teeth and drop it between the sickles. The magpie, at last, files the case under Legs. Late, but just.

fail.log: You find nothing but mud and an old sandal. The villages fight anyway. Two men are hurt. You stop it with a roar, and that is all you can do. (-8 health)

choices.text: Roar them apart and let them sort it out themselves

effects.log: They go home without their sickles. They do not sort it out. They will be back.

events.text: An autumn night on the flat rock, the court empty. The Three Stars climb out of the west, three in a line, straight as a beam, and the three small ones hang beneath. You have felt it since the first case: something in your chest that tips. Every pardon lifts one end. Every punishment lowers the other.

choices.text: Lean toward mercy. The world has enough teeth

effects.log: You decide to err kind. The magpie, on the branch, makes a small noise that might be approval and might be a warning.

choices.text: Lean toward severity. Autumn is the season of iron

effects.log: You decide to err hard. The three small stars seem, for a moment, a little brighter.

choices.text: Hold it level, and feel how heavy that is

effects.log: You do not lean. It costs more than leaning either way, and it will every autumn for the rest of your life. Your grandmother, if you have met her, would call it the beam with a stone on each end.

events.text: A case under Stomach, the mansion of granaries. A famine spring in the lower village. A widow with three children took a sack of rice from the headman's storehouse at night and was caught with it on her back. The headman wants her hands broken. The magpie, on its branch, mentions that the storehouse is full, and that the relief rice the county sent in the winter went into it, and never came out.

choices.text: Pardon the widow; make the headman open the storehouse to the whole village

effects.log: The headman opens the storehouse with a tiger sitting in his yard. Every family gets a measure. The magpie files the case under Stomach, Heaven's Granary. It was just.

choices.text: Punish the widow. Theft is theft

effects.log: The widow goes home with her hands bound and no rice. The headman thanks the mountain with a pig's head. The magpie writes it down and files it nowhere, and will not look at you all winter.

choices.text: Go and smell the storehouse yourself before you judge

ok.log: The county's rice still smells of the county's sacks. You lie down across the storehouse door until the headman gives it all back, and a little more. The widow keeps her sack. Filed under Stomach. It was just.

fail.log: The storehouse smells of rice, and rats, and nothing else you can read. You let the widow go and leave the headman alone, and the next famine is the same. Not filed.

events.text: A case under Net, the mansion of hunters. Two brothers from the charcoal village have been snaring deer in the old man's own grove, where nobody hunts. They say their families are hungry, and that is true. The magpie adds that they set the snares along the path the children take to gather acorns, and that a girl of seven lost her foot in one last month, and that the brothers moved the snares and said nothing.

choices.text: Punish them: every snare dug up by their hands, and the girl's family fed for a year from their hunting

effects.log: A year of hard labour, and the brothers know a tiger watches every day of it. The girl's family eats meat all winter. Filed under Net. It was just.

choices.text: Pardon them. Hungry men set snares

effects.log: The brothers go home relieved. A month later they set new snares, further from the grove, and not further from the children's path. The magpie files it nowhere.

choices.text: Take them both. Snares on a children's path deserve a tiger

effects.log: Two ghosts follow you out of the grove, still arguing about whose snare it was. The village is very quiet for a long time. The magpie does not file it anywhere, and the old man under the pine does not speak to you that winter.

events.text: A case under Bond, the mansion of crowds. In the dry summer a mob from three villages burned the hut of a fortune-teller, an outsider, for bringing the drought with a curse. The fortune-teller got out with burns. Now the crowd stands in your clearing, forty people, sullen and frightened, and none of them will say who started it. The magpie knows: a rice merchant who owed the fortune-teller a great deal of money, and went from house to house the night before.

choices.text: Punish the merchant who lit the crowd; pardon the crowd, and make them rebuild the hut

effects.log: Forty people rebuild a hut in nine days, very fast, with a tiger supervising. The merchant pays the debt twice over, and leaves the district. Filed under Bond. It was just.

choices.text: Punish all forty. They all carried a torch

effects.log: Forty households fined, beaten, shamed. The merchant, who carried no torch, is among the loudest to agree. The magpie writes it down and files it nowhere.

choices.text: Pardon all forty. A crowd is nobody

effects.log: The crowd goes home. Next drought, it finds another outsider. The magpie files it nowhere.

events.text: A case under Hairy Head, the mansion of the gathering in white: a funeral. Two brothers in mourning hemp stand in your clearing with the coffin of their father on a bier between them. The elder has dug a grave by night on the sunny shoulder of a hill that belongs to another family's ancestors, because a geomancer said it was the best site in the county. The other family has found it and is coming with hoes to dig it up. The younger brother says nothing, and will not meet your eye.

choices.text: Order the grave moved to the brothers' own hill; pardon the younger, who only obeyed

effects.log: The father is buried again, on his own family's plain hill, with a tiger lying at the head of the grave through the whole rite so nobody quarrels. The other family's hill is left in peace. Filed under Hairy Head. It was just.

choices.text: Let the grave stay where it is. The dead should not be dug up

effects.log: The father lies in stolen ground. The other family goes to the county court, and the case goes on for years, and costs both families everything. The magpie files it nowhere.

choices.text: Ask the younger brother why he will not look at you

ok.log: Because, he says at last, the father asked to be buried beside the mother, on the poor family hill, and the elder burned the letter. The grave goes back beside the mother. The elder is sent away to mourn alone. Filed under Hairy Head. It was just.

fail.log: He will not speak. You order the grave moved anyway, and it is, but you are not sure you knew why. Not filed.

events.text: Autumn, and the flat rock, and the season's small cases: a stolen hen, a boundary stone moved one pace in the night, a mother-in-law who poured lye in the soup. The magpie reads them out one by one in a bored voice.

choices.text: Pardon the lot of them; it is a good harvest

effects.log: A good harvest, a soft court. The villages go home happy. The mother-in-law looks thoughtful in a way you do not like.

choices.text: Punish the lot of them; small wrongs grow

effects.log: A hard court for small wrongs. The villages go home quiet. The boundary stone goes back its pace, and two more stones move in other villages, out of spite.

choices.text: Take each case on its own, slowly, until the moon sets

effects.log: Hen: pardoned, a fox did it. Stone: punished. Lye: a long talk with the mother-in-law, at the end of which the mother-in-law is crying and the daughter-in-law is laughing, and you are not sure how either happened.

events.text: The magpie brings you a case out of season, in spring, which it is not supposed to do. In the valley below the west ridge, a grown son, {npc}, beats the old mother who raised {him} alone; the neighbours hear it through the walls and do nothing, because it is family business. The old man under the pine, when you ask, only says: "Not yet. Watch. It is not your season for that one."
events.arc: The Son Who Beat His Mother

choices.text: Watch, as the old man says

effects.log: You lie in the bamboo behind the house for a month of evenings. You see more than the neighbours do. You do not like any of it.

choices.text: Go down now and put the fear of the mountain into {him}

effects.log: {npc} wakes to a tiger in the yard and screams the house down. For a month the beatings stop. Then they start again, quieter, with the shutters closed. The old man says nothing. That is the reproach.

choices.text: Tell the magpie to file it under the Three Stars, and wait

effects.log: The magpie writes it on the inside of its head, where it keeps everything, and does not say anything clever for a whole day.

events.text: What you see from the bamboo: the old mother hides the bruises from the neighbours with a long sleeve, sets aside the best of the rice for {npc} and eats the scorched crust from the bottom of the pot. When {npc} comes home angry from the tavern the old mother warms the floor first. When the village headman asks, the answer is always a fall on the ice.
events.arc: The Son Who Beat His Mother

choices.text: Leave a hare on the step every few days, so the old mother eats

effects.log: The old mother finds the hares and cooks them for {npc}. Of course. You keep leaving them anyway, and the third time you see the old mother eat a little too, standing up, quickly, when nobody is looking.

choices.text: Follow {npc} to the tavern and see what kind of man is in there

effects.log: {npc} owes money to everyone in the tavern and is laughed at by all of them, and comes home and beats the one person who never laughs. It explains everything. It excuses nothing.

events.text: Night, and {npc} goes out to the privy behind the house with a lamp, muttering. You are waiting on the far side of the brushwood fence. You can speak now. You have not yet decided what to say.
events.arc: The Son Who Beat His Mother

choices.text: Say one sentence, very low: "The mountain is watching that old woman"

mem.note: warned me from behind the fence

ok.log: {npc} drops the lamp. For a year the house is silent. Not kind; silent. It is not enough, and it is not nothing, and the old man under the pine nods when you tell it, and says, "Later."

fail.log: {npc} runs inside and drinks until dawn and tells the whole tavern next day that the tiger spoke. Nobody believes it. The old mother does, and is frightened for {him}, which is the worst of all.

choices.text: Say nothing. Show {him} your face over the fence, in the lamplight

effects.log: The lamp goes out. In the morning {npc} has gone white at the temples, overnight, and does not touch the old mother for a long time. When it starts again, it is worse.

events.text: Under the pine, the old man of the mountain finally talks about {npc}. "This one is the hardest kind," the old man says. "Too little and the mother dies of it. Too much and you are only another son who beats someone. When the white comes into your tail, it will be your errand. Until then, keep watching, and keep the mother fed."
events.arc: The Son Who Beat His Mother

choices.text: "I will be ready"

effects.log: You go back to the bamboo behind the house. It is a long watch. You will be there, one way or another, when the white comes.

choices.text: "Why make me wait?"

effects.log: "Because now you would kill," the old man says, "and you would be right, and it would be wrong. Wait until you can do the right thing and not enjoy it."

events.text: The guest has come to the village under the pass. Nobody says the word for the sickness; they say the honoured guest, politely, so as not to offend it. Every house has stopped sweeping and stopped quarrelling and stopped cooking anything with a strong smell. In every yard a bowl of clean water stands on the jar platform for the guest to drink. And on every gate, fresh-pasted, a painting of a tiger: crossed eyes, a grin, very fierce, very badly drawn. In one house a child is burning with fever.

choices.text: Walk the lanes at night, slowly, so the painted tigers have a real one behind them

effects.log: Every night for a month, a tiger in the lanes between the gates. Nobody sees you; everybody knows. The children in the fever-house say the guest left by the back gate in a hurry. Only one child of the village dies that winter, where in the next valley it is nine.

choices.text: Roar down the valley, once, to drive it out

ok.log: The fever breaks in three houses the next morning. The shaman scolds the village for letting a tiger shout at an honoured guest, and is secretly very relieved.

fail.log: The fever does not care how loud you are. The village, frightened twice over, sends for the tiger-catchers as well as the shaman.

choices.text: Keep away. Even a tiger is polite to that guest

effects.log: You stay up on the ridge. The guest stays its season, as the guest does, and leaves when it chooses. The village counts its dead and its pocked faces in the spring, and so do you.

events.text: The sending-off. The shaman has made a horse of straw, saddled it with a bag of rice cakes and a little money, and the whole village walks it to the edge of the fields at dawn, singing, bowing, begging the honoured guest to ride away in comfort and not look back. The road the straw horse faces goes up to your pass.

choices.text: Escort the guest politely over the pass and down the far side

effects.log: You walk in front of an empty straw horse all the way over the pass and down to the river, very formally. The thing riding it is cold and hot at once and watches the back of your neck the whole way. At the river it goes on alone. You are feverish for a week. (-6 health)

choices.text: Lie across the road. The guest goes back the way it came, to the sea

ok.log: The straw horse stops on the road below you as if it had walked into a wall. In the morning it is found turned round, facing the sea, and the next village up the pass never gets the guest at all.

fail.log: The guest does not go round. It goes through. You are ill a whole season in the den, hot and cold, and the next village up the pass gets it anyway. (-14 health)

choices.text: Eat the rice cakes off the straw horse

effects.log: It seemed a waste. You are very ill for a month, and you deserved it, and the magpie tells everyone.

events.text: Twenty years on, a pock-faced woodcarver from the village under the pass carves tigers: on gateposts, on spoons, on the lids of rice chests. Every one has crossed eyes and a grin, and every one, if you look closely, is walking slowly down a lane at night.

choices.text: Leave a whisker on the carver's doorstep

effects.log: The carver finds it and does not say anything to anybody, and carves it into the lid of a chest in thin gold lacquer, and keeps that chest until the end.

choices.text: Let it be. Some debts are already paid

effects.log: The tigers go on, gate after gate, crossed eyes and all. They are the best guards the valley has, and you never touch a single one.

events.text: A folk painter, a wandering one with a bundle of brushes and a pot of soot ink, has set up by the village gate before the New Year to paint the pictures people paste on their gates: a magpie on a pine, a tiger below. He has seen you on the ridge. He wants a sitting. He has already painted the magpie, and the magpie, on the real pine above, looks smug.

choices.text: Sit on the rock across the lane, quite still, and be painted

effects.log: He paints for an hour, very fast, laughing to himself. When he turns the paper round you see: crossed eyes, a mouth full of grin, paws like dumplings, and the magpie lecturing you from the pine. It is you exactly, the way a yangban looks to a farmer.

choices.text: Scare him off his stool

effects.log: He goes over backwards into the snow with the brush still in his mouth. That year every tiger he paints has its fur standing on end and its eyes popping out, which sells much better.

choices.text: Laugh, the way tigers laugh, and walk off

effects.log: He paints you laughing. It is the only tiger picture in the province where the tiger is in on the joke, and it hangs on the headman's gate for years.

events.text: New Year's morning: down the whole lane, gate after gate, you. Crossed eyes, a grin, dumpling paws. And on every single one the magpie, on the pine, lecturing you. The children run up and down the lane pointing at the gates and then up at the ridge, and the real magpie sits on the real pine above your real head and laughs and laughs.

choices.text: Let them laugh. A tiger on every gate keeps evil out

effects.log: Evil, as it happens, does not cross that village all year. Neither do any bandits. The pictures are ridiculous. They also work.

choices.text: Knock the magpie off its branch

ok.log: You get a tail feather. The magpie gets a new joke, which it tells to the entire mountain.

fail.log: You miss, and fall off the rock into the snowdrift, in front of the whole village. Next year's pictures show it.

events.text: The folk painter is old, and has walked up the pass one last time to the shrine with a roll of paper under his arm. He unrolls it on the step and weighs it down with stones. A tiger and a magpie, as always. But this time the tiger is not ridiculous. It is lying on a rock above a road at dusk, and it is watching over a line of ten woodcutters going home, and it is you.

choices.text: Lie down beside the painting until he goes

effects.log: He sits on the step and the two of you look at it together for a long time. Then he leaves it at the shrine and goes down the mountain and does not come back. It hangs in the shrine for two hundred years, until the damp gets it.

choices.text: Put your paw on it, gently, for a seal

effects.log: One clear pawprint in the corner, where a painter puts a seal. He laughs until he cries. That painting goes to a collector in the capital, and the collector never believes the story, and keeps it anyway.

events.text: The old man walks you to the edge of a valley you have never seen. A mountain behind it like a back to lean on, a stream in front that winds round like an arm. Two long ridges come down on either side, holding the valley floor between them like two hands holding a bowl. Nobody lives in it. "Every good place," the old man says, "has a tiger on its right hand. This one has had nothing for a long time. Lie down."

choices.text: Lie down along the right ridge

effects.log: You lie down along the pale rock of the right ridge, and it fits. Your shoulders where the ridge rises, your flank along the pines, your tail down to the stream. When you wake, months later, the ridge has your shape and you have its. You are the right ridge now.

choices.text: Walk the whole valley first, both sides

effects.log: You walk it for a season: the stream, the floor, the empty left ridge with its dark pines, the saddle between. Then you lie down along the right one, because the old man was right, and because it already smells of you.

choices.text: Mark every tree on the right ridge first

effects.log: Every tree from the saddle to the stream. There is nobody to read the marks. You make them anyway. A ridge is a kind of territory, and you are still a tiger.

events.text: On the west side of your ridge, under the bracken, you find what is left of people who lived here once and went away: three flat stones set one on two, an old altar, and a broken bowl. And under a slab of rock a little way up, a spring, cold and deep, that no human has found and no deer has found either. It tastes of iron. It tastes of autumn.

choices.text: Keep the spring hidden. Some day the valley will need it

effects.log: You put the slab back and let the bracken grow over it. A spring nobody has found yet. You will keep it a very long time, for a very bad year.

choices.text: Drink from it every autumn, and nobody else

effects.log: Iron water, cold as a blade. Every autumn you drink, and every autumn your stripes come in darker and your breath comes out colder.

choices.text: Clean the old altar and set the broken bowl on it

effects.log: An altar for nobody, in a valley of nobody. The old man of the mountain, passing, stops and looks at it and does not say anything, which you have learned is approval.

events.text: A family of travellers comes up the valley with an ox and a cart: hill farmers looking for land. They walk the valley floor all day. They look at the stream and the soil and the two ridges. At dusk the father shakes his head. "Too empty," he says. "Nobody lives here. There must be a reason." They go on over the pass.

choices.text: Let them go. The valley will fill when it is ready

effects.log: The cart goes over the pass. The valley stays empty, and you stay on the right ridge, and the left stays dark. Since before the first house was built, you think. It has a ring to it.

choices.text: Show yourself on the ridge, so they know the reason

effects.log: The father looks up and sees what the reason is, and makes the cart go over the pass much faster. It will be a long time before anyone tries this valley again.

choices.text: Walk down at night and leave a deer by their cart, as a welcome

effects.log: In the morning there is a deer by the cart and a pug mark the size of a winnowing basket. The father thinks about it all through breakfast, and then goes on over the pass anyway. A gift from a tiger is still a tiger.

events.text: A winter night, clear and very cold. From your ridge you look across the valley at the left ridge, as you do most nights. It is dark, and empty, and the pines on it stand very still. The old man of the mountain has come up to sit beside you for once. "Something is coming for that side," he says. "Not this century. Maybe the next. When it comes, try to be civil."

choices.text: "I will be civil"

effects.log: "Good," he says. "It will not be." He seems to find that funny. You lie awake after he has gone, looking at the dark ridge across the valley, wondering what has no manners and is coming to live opposite you.

choices.text: "It will be civil to me. I was here first"

effects.log: "Since before the first house was built," the old man says. "Yes. Say that to it. Say it just like that." He is laughing at you, and you do not know why yet.

events.text: On the lower slope of your ridge, a new grave mound, and beside it a hut of straw and sticks no bigger than a dog-kennel. In it, {npc}, in coarse undyed hemp, with a straw mat and a wooden pillow, who has come to live by a parent's grave for three years, eat no meat, drink no liquor, hear no music, and mourn. The old man of the mountain comes to stand beside you. "Guard the hut," the old man says. "Three winters. That is your errand."

choices.text: Lie down by the hut door the first night

effects.log: {npc} sees you in the morning across the threshold, and goes very still, and then, because there is nothing else to do and the rites must go on, bows to the grave and lights the incense. You do not move. Neither does {npc}. It is the beginning.

choices.text: Guard from the ridge, unseen

effects.log: You lie on the ridge above the hut, where you can see the grave and the road and the forest. {npc} never sees you. The wolves do.

choices.text: "Three years, for one human?"

effects.log: "For a human doing the same," the old man says. You go down to the hut, chastened, and lie in the snow where you can see it.

events.text: Bandits in the first autumn. Somebody has told them a rich family buried its dead on the ridge, and rich families bury silver, and the mourner in the hut is only one person with a hemp hood and no sword. Four of them come up the slope at dusk with shovels and a lamp.

choices.text: Stand up at the hut door and speak: "This hut is the mountain god's"

effects.log: A tiger that talks. The bandits drop the shovels. One of them drops the lamp. {npc}, behind you, drops the incense. The bandits are three valleys away by midnight. {npc} does not sleep at all, and in the morning bows to you, as well as to the grave.

choices.text: Go down the slope to meet them

ok.log: They have shovels. You have the rest. They leave the shovels, which {npc} uses that winter to clear the snow.

fail.log: One of them has a spear under the shovels. You drive them off, but you lie bleeding in the bracken for a week, and while you lie there they come back for the grave goods and beat {npc} and burn the hut. (-18 health)

choices.text: Roar from the ridge

effects.log: Four bandits run. So, nearly, does {npc}, before remembering that a mourner does not leave the grave, and sitting back down, shaking, in the doorway of the hut.

events.text: The second winter, and the snow has buried the hut to the eaves. Every morning {npc} digs out the doorway and the path to the grave, lights the incense, bows, and then sets down a second bowl of thin millet gruel in the snow by the door. For you. A mourner eats no meat; it has never occurred to {npc} that a tiger might mind.

choices.text: Eat the gruel

effects.log: It is thin and hot and tastes of almost nothing. You eat it every morning for the rest of the winter. {npc} begins to talk to you while you eat, about the dead parent, a little more each day.

choices.text: Lie against the hut wall all night, so the straw stays warm

effects.log: A tiger is a great deal of warmth. The hut, with you against it, is the warmest place on the mountain. {npc} sleeps through the night for the first time since the funeral. (-8 health)

choices.text: Speak to {him}, through the straw, at night

mem.note: talked to me through the wall

effects.log: A tiger and a mourner, talking through a straw wall in the snow, all winter: about grief, about rice, about whether the dead are cold. You have never talked so much in your life. Neither, it turns out, has {npc}.

events.text: The third spring. The mourning is over. {npc} takes off the hemp, washes in the stream, bows to the grave a last time and pulls down the hut with {his} own hands. Then {npc} turns to you, standing where you have stood for three winters, and does not know what to say.

choices.text: Walk beside {him} all the way to the village gate

effects.log: A whole village sees a mourner come home after three years with a tiger walking beside, like a dog, like a friend. At the gate you stop. {npc} bows, and goes in. Up on the summit an old man sets down a pipe. The errand is done.

choices.text: Say one thing to {him}: "Your parent was well guarded"

mem.note: said my parent was well guarded

effects.log: {npc} kneels in the wet grass and weeps, at last, for the first time in three years; a mourner is not supposed to, much, during the rites. You stay until it is done. The errand is done.

choices.text: Leave before {he} turns round, and leave a whisker on the grave

effects.log: When {npc} turns round there is nobody there, only a long white-tipped whisker on the grave mound. It goes into the family shrine, in a lacquer box, and the family never sells it, whatever the offers. The errand is done.

events.text: Another grave on your ridge, another straw hut, another mourner in hemp: the old man of the mountain has found you a second chance, because you failed the first. "Three winters," he says. "Again."

choices.text: Lie down at the hut door, and do not move for three years

ok.log: Three winters, three summers, bandits twice, wolves often, snow to the eaves. You are thinner at the end of it and the mourner is alive and whole. The errand is done. (-10 health)

fail.log: In the second winter a fever takes the mourner, and you can do nothing against that. The hut comes down. The old man says only, "Again, then." (-12 health)

choices.text: Guard from the ridge, and teach the wolves the hut is yours

effects.log: Every wolf, fox and bandit on the mountain learns, one way or another, not to go near that hut. The mourner never sees you, and lives through all three winters wondering why the mountain is so quiet. The errand is done.

events.text: A winter morning, and the magpie is pecking at your tail. You turn to snap at it and stop. At the very tip, where the last black ring should be, there are white hairs. Not grey; white, like new snow, like the old man's beard. The magpie holds one up in its beak, very pleased, and flies off to tell everyone.
events.arc: The White at the Tail's Tip

choices.text: Lie still and look at it a long time

effects.log: White. The old tigers say a tiger whitens toward its five hundredth year. You are not nearly that. Something in you is in a hurry, and you do not know what.

choices.text: Roll in the mud to hide it

effects.log: It comes out white again in the first rain. Some things will not be hidden. The magpie tells the whole mountain anyway.

events.text: The white has spread a hand's width up your tail. In the village under the pass people have started saying it: the tiger of the pass has a white tail. Old women touch their foreheads. A boy is sent to the county town to tell the magistrate. A white tiger is an omen, everyone knows; nobody agrees of what.
events.arc: The White at the Tail's Tip

choices.text: Let them talk. An omen is a kind of shelter

effects.log: The talk spreads. A white tail on the mountain means a good year, says one fortune-teller; a bad one, says another. The harvest is ordinary. You are not.

choices.text: Stay off the pass for a few years and let them forget

effects.log: They do not forget. They embroider. By the time you come back you are pure white, ten paces long and speak in verse.

events.text: A tuft of white from your tail caught on a thornbush by the pass has found its way to the county market, and to {npc}, a dealer in furs, who holds it up to the light and goes very quiet. A striped pelt is worth a house. A white one has never been sold, because there has never been one; the court would pay for it whatever was asked. {npc} starts asking questions at the inns.
events.arc: The Price of a White Tail

choices.text: Let {him} ask. A merchant is not a hunter

effects.log: {npc} asks for a month and learns where the pass is and whose rock is above the bend. A merchant is not a hunter. A merchant can hire hunters.

choices.text: Go into the town at night and leave a pawprint on {his} stall

effects.log: {npc} finds a pawprint as big as a winnowing basket on the counter in the morning, right on top of the tuft. {npc} sits down and thinks about it for a long time. Then raises the price.

events.text: {npc} has hired three trappers and bought a pig. The pig has been staked out on your ridge, and it is full of something bitter you can smell from the saddle, a poison root the trappers boil down. Around it, in a ring, iron jaws under the leaves.
events.arc: The Price of a White Tail

choices.text: Leave the pig. Spring every trap with a branch

effects.log: Nine traps go off one after another with a noise like a smithy. The trappers come up in the morning and find a ring of sprung iron round a pig nobody has touched, and go and ask {npc} for more money.

choices.text: Carry the poisoned pig down to {his} stall and drop it at the door

ok.log: A dead poisoned pig on the step of the fur stall, its rope still on, and a single white hair laid on top of it. {npc} closes the stall for the season. The trappers go home.

fail.log: One trap you missed. You get it off your foreleg in the end, and carry the pig down anyway, limping. (-15 health)

events.text: {npc} is at the shrine on the pass, alone, at dusk, with a lamp. {He} has heard that the tiger of the pass can speak now. "I will be honest," {npc} says to the dark. "The court will pay a magistrate's yearly stipend for a white pelt. I could live like a lord. I have three children and a bad roof. What would you do, in my place?"
events.arc: The Price of a White Tail

choices.text: Speak: "I would look for a smaller roof"

mem.note: spoke to me at the shrine

effects.log: {npc} laughs, startled, then sits down on the shrine step and keeps laughing. "Yes," {npc} says. "All right." The trappers are paid off. {npc} goes back to fox and marten, and tells the story at the inns until everybody is sick of it.

choices.text: Speak: "Come and take it"

effects.log: {npc} goes white and goes home. Not for good. Somewhere a ledger has a white pelt written in it, with a price, and that ledger will outlive {npc}.

choices.text: Say nothing; show {him} the white tip in the lamplight, and go

effects.log: {npc} looks at the white for a long time after you have gone. The next spring {npc} paints it, very badly, on the sign of the fur stall: a tiger with a white tail, and under it, no price.

events.text: The spring festival at the great temple in the valley: from the eighth night of the second month to the fifteenth, people walk round the stone pagoda all night with lanterns, round and round, each one making a wish. You walk with them, in a human shape that does not quite fit at the shoulders. Round and round. And one of the young hwarang, the flower youths with the feathered hats, {npc}, keeps pace with you, round after round, and at the turn by the bell pavilion, looks across and smiles.

choices.text: Keep pace, and speak

mem.note: circled the pagoda with me all night

effects.log: Your first words to a human in a human mouth: something about the cold. {npc} answers with something about the lanterns. By dawn you have gone round the pagoda nine hundred times and neither of you has made a wish, because you were talking.

choices.text: Ask what {he} is wishing for

mem.note: asked my wish at the pagoda

effects.log: "To be useful," {npc} says. "To matter to something. Isn't that stupid?" You do not think so. You do not say so either. You walk round the pagoda together until the bell.

choices.text: Turn and walk round the other way

effects.log: Now you meet face to face at every turn instead of side by side. That is worse. {npc} laughs out loud at the third meeting, and so, to your horror, do you.

events.text: The next spring festival, and {npc} is waiting at the same corner of the pagoda with two lanterns, one for you. Round and round all night again, and talk, and at dawn, by the bell pavilion, {npc} asks the question you knew was coming: your name, your village, your family.

choices.text: Tell a true thing: "From the mountain to the west. My family is large and quarrelsome"

mem.note: told me about the mountain to the west

effects.log: {npc} laughs. "Mine too," {npc} says. Neither of you knows yet how much you are both telling the truth.

choices.text: Invent a village and a family

effects.log: A village three valleys east, a father who sells salt. {npc} believes every word. You find the lie heavier to carry than anything you have ever carried in your teeth.

choices.text: Vanish at dawn without answering

effects.log: {npc} turns round and you are gone, and there is a single white hair on the lantern you held. {npc} keeps it.

events.text: Your three littermates come across your bounds in the spring, all three together: bigger than you, older-smelling, with human blood on their breath. They have kept eating what you never would. They circle you and sniff, and the biggest one laughs. "You stink of temple incense," it says, "and of a human's sleeve. Which human? We would like to meet it."

choices.text: Tell them nothing

effects.log: They circle you until dusk and then go off laughing. They will find out. They always found the best of the carcass first, too.

choices.text: Warn them: touch that one, and you will hunt them

ok.log: One of them tests you. It goes home bleeding. The other two look at you differently, and leave the temple valley alone. For now.

fail.log: Three to one. They leave you in the snow with your ear torn, laughing, and now they know there is something to find. (-20 health)

choices.text: Laugh it off: a festival, a crowd, nobody

effects.log: "Nobody," says the biggest, licking its lips. "Nobody smells very nice." They go. You do not sleep that night.

events.text: After the festival {npc} follows you, quietly, out of the temple gate and up the valley road, all the way to the edge of the forest where you always say goodbye. "I want to see where you live," {npc} says. "Just once." The trees are dark. You can feel your human shape thinning at the edges.

choices.text: Let {him} see

mem.note: saw what my friend from the pagoda really is

effects.log: You let the shape go. {npc} stands in the road in front of a tiger, white at the tail, and does not run. After a very long time {npc} says, "Oh," and then, "Of course," and then, quite steadily, "Does it hurt, changing?" It does. Nobody has ever asked.

choices.text: Slip into the trees and be gone

effects.log: {npc} calls after you twice, then stands in the road until dark, and goes back to the temple alone, and is there again at the next festival, waiting at the same corner.

choices.text: Speak from the dark, in your own voice

mem.note: heard the voice from the forest

effects.log: Your own voice is deeper than the human one, and comes from much lower down, and from a long way inside the trees. {npc} goes pale. Then {npc} says, "I knew it was something," and walks home without looking back, which is either courage or love.

events.text: In a roadside inn below the temple, {npc} tells you the news, proud and frightened at once: the court has sent {his} band of flower youths to the southern hills, to hunt three man-eating tigers that have killed eleven people this year. Three, all from one litter. {npc} will lead the second company. "If I come back," {npc} says, "they will give me a rank."

choices.text: Warn your littermates to go north

effects.log: You run all night to tell them. The three of them listen, and laugh, and do not go north. Eleven humans is nothing, the biggest says. Let the flower youths come.

choices.text: Ask {npc} not to go

mem.note: begged me not to hunt the tigers

ok.log: {npc} looks at you a long time, puzzled, then hurt, then, slowly, as if understanding something {he} does not want to: "All right. Not this year." The flower youths go south without {him}. The three are not found.

fail.log: "It is what a hwarang is for," {npc} says, gently, as if you were a child. "You would not understand." You understand better than anyone alive.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let heaven sort tigers from humans

effects.log: You drink, and {npc} talks, and you say nothing at all, and the flower youths go south. Whatever happens in the southern hills will happen without you, this time.

events.text: The last night of the spring festival. {npc} stops you at the corner by the bell pavilion and puts something in your hand: a pin of plain silver, the kind a hwarang wears in the topknot. "Whatever you are," {npc} says. "Whatever your family is. I want to circle this pagoda with you every spring until I am too old to walk. Will you come?"

choices.text: "Every spring"

mem.note: promised me every spring at the pagoda

effects.log: You close your hand on the pin. It is the first thing a human has ever given you that you keep. Somewhere in the southern hills three tigers lift their heads at the same moment, as if they had smelled something.

choices.text: Give the pin back. A tiger cannot promise springs

effects.log: {npc} takes it back without a word and goes round the pagoda alone until dawn. You watch from the dark under the bell pavilion. It is the right thing. It does not feel like any kind of thing at all.

choices.text: Tell {him} everything: the tigers in the south are your littermates

mem.note: told me whose litter the man-eaters were

effects.log: {npc} listens to all of it, the den, the three, the eleven dead, with a face like stone. At the end {npc} closes your hand round the pin. "Then we will have to be very careful," {npc} says. "Both of us."

events.text: A roadside inn at the foot of your pass: a yard, a low table, a jar of milky rice liquor, a pot of soup that has been boiling since the old king's time. You sit in your human shape at the table and {npc}, who keeps the inn, talks without stopping: about salt prices, about the headman, about the tiger of the pass, which ate a whole salt carrier last year, everyone knows, though nobody can say which one.

choices.text: Agree that the tiger is a menace

effects.log: You agree. You agree so warmly that {npc} gives you a second bowl of soup free. On the way out you find yourself annoyed on the tiger's behalf, which is a new feeling and not a comfortable one.

choices.text: Say you have heard it carries children home at night

effects.log: "Oh, that too," {npc} says, without any trouble at all. "It does both. It is a tiger." You walk back up the mountain thinking that is the best description of you anyone has ever given.

choices.text: Ask {him} what the pass would be without its tiger

effects.log: {npc} thinks about it, stirring the soup. "Full of robbers," {npc} says. "And I would sell no beds. Do not tell it I said so."

events.text: At the gate of the county office, a petitioner, {npc}, has been sitting for three days with a written complaint that nobody will take. You sit down beside {him} in your human shape. The complaint is about the tiger bounty: the magistrate's nephew collects it every year for tigers killed on mountains where no tiger has eaten anyone, and the hunters who do the work get a sack of millet.

choices.text: Help {him} rewrite it so it cannot be ignored

ok.log: You know more about tigers than the whole county office put together, and it shows. The petition goes in on the fourth day and comes out again on the fortieth, with a seal on it. The nephew goes away for a while.

fail.log: You do not know the forms. Nobody does but the clerks. The petition goes in and is lost, as petitions are.

choices.text: Listen, and remember every name

effects.log: The nephew, two hunters, a fur dealer, a clerk with a crooked thumb. You will not forget any of them. Tigers have long memories, and a long time to use them.

choices.text: Walk past the nephew's house that night in your other shape

effects.log: The nephew sees a tiger in the lane, looking at the family gate, and the petitioner's complaint is answered with remarkable speed. It is not the kind of justice the magpie files.

events.text: Market day, and a small child selling straw sandals from a mat, {npc}, looks up at you and stops in the middle of a price. "You are the tiger," {npc} says, quite loudly. "You have the eyes." Three people turn round.

choices.text: Laugh and buy every pair of sandals on the mat

effects.log: Twelve pairs of straw sandals. You have nowhere to put them and no feet that fit them. {npc} goes home early and very rich and tells everyone the tiger bought sandals, and nobody believes it, and that is your disguise.

choices.text: Crouch down and say, very quietly, "Yes. Do not tell"

effects.log: {npc} nods, enormously serious, and keeps the secret for years, and tells it at the very end to a grandchild, who keeps it too.

choices.text: Say "What a strange child" and walk on

effects.log: The three people turn back to their business. {npc} watches you all the way out of the market, unconvinced.

events.text: In a village yard a shaman, {npc}, is in the middle of a rite, bells and fan and a drum, and stops dead as you pass the gate in your human shape. The drum stops. The shaman comes out into the lane, kneels in the dust in front of you and says, loud enough for the whole village: "The Mountain Lord has come down!"

choices.text: Raise {him} up and ask {him} to finish the rite

effects.log: You stand at the back of the yard while the rite goes on, and the drum is better than it has ever been, and the sick old man in the house sits up at the end of it. Whether that was you, or the shaman, or the rite, nobody can say. {npc} will say, for the rest of {his} life.

choices.text: Say "You are mistaken, I sell salt," and keep walking

effects.log: {npc} stays kneeling in the lane until you are out of sight, and the village decides the shaman has gone mad, and the shaman does not care.

choices.text: Ask {him} how {he} knew

effects.log: "You walk like the mountain is following you," {npc} says. "Because it is." You go back up the ridge that night and look behind you all the way.

events.text: An old soldier, {npc}, on a bench outside the post-station, missing two fingers to frost, talks to anyone who will sit. You sit. {He} has served at the forts on the great river in the north, where the winter is half the year, and the raiders come over the ice, and the tigers, {he} says, are bigger than oxen and dark as smoke.

choices.text: Ask about the tigers beyond the river

effects.log: {npc} tells you about them for an hour: a tigress who walks along the far bank every winter looking south. You do not say anything. You wonder who the tigress is looking for.

choices.text: Ask about the soldiers at the fort

effects.log: Rations sold by the commanders, coats sold, men who walk away and are hanged for it. {npc} spits. "The raiders are not the worst thing on that river," {npc} says. You will remember that when the white comes in and armies want your banner.

choices.text: Buy {him} a bowl of soup and just listen

effects.log: Nobody has bought {npc} soup in ten years. {npc} talks until the post-horses come, and at the end grips your hand with the three fingers that are left.

events.text: A blind fortune-teller, {npc}, at a crossroads with a mat and a bamboo cup of sticks, catches your sleeve as you pass. "Sit," {npc} says. "I have not read a face like that in forty years." {He} runs dry fingers over your face in your human shape, and stops at the eyes, and is silent a long time.

choices.text: "What do you see?"

effects.log: "A beam," {npc} says. "With a stone on each end. And a long road, all of it uphill. And something white. Do not ask me what. I am only a fortune-teller." {He} will not take your money.

choices.text: Pull away before {he} can say it

effects.log: {npc} laughs behind you all the way down the road. "You cannot pull away from a face," {npc} calls. "You have to wear it home."
